utterances.text: Please be seated. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14-A, the Prosecution versus Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can everyone hear me? Good morning to everyone. Can everybody hear me? The interpreters? The appellant? Can the appellant hear me? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The Defence, Prosecution? So I would like to call for the appearances of the parties. I turn first to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of appellant, Russell Hayman, with my co-counsel to my left, Anto Nobilo, Andrew Paley, and Robert Perrin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for the Prosecution is Norman Farrell, Ms. Sonja Boelaert-Suominen, Ms. Michelle Jarvis, Ms. Marie-Ursula Kind, and Ms. Kelly Howick. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand -- I've been told that the health of the appellant is not very well. May I ask the Defence if that's correct, and then perhaps the appellant himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we can proceed this morning, but I think we would be derelict in not informing Your Honours of certain health information regarding the appellant. And I think it would be most appropriate if we go into private session for just a moment. I think this will only take a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go into closed session for a couple of minutes. Sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. As announced by the registrar, this case is the Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic. Last week, the evidentiary portion of this hearing took place, and six Defence witnesses gave their testimony before the Appeals Chamber. The evidentiary portion of this hearing has been completed. We will now hear the final arguments of the parties in this appeal. In its judgement, rendered on the 3rd of March, 2000, the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Blaskic of 19 counts, set forth in the indictment. These counts encompassed violation of Articles 2, 3, and 5 of the Statute. Mr. Blaskic was not found guilty of Count 2, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3(B) of the Statute. Furthermore, in relation to Counts 3 and 4, he was found not guilty. Mr. Blaskic was found guilty for having ordered the crimes, and the Trial Chamber also stated in the disposition of the judgement that in any event, as a commander, he failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures which would have allowed these crimes to be prevented or the perpetrators thereof to be punished. The Trial Chamber imposed a single sentence of 45 years imprisonment. The Defence filed its notice of appeal against the judgement on 17 March 2000. Due to decisions suspending the briefing schedule on 19 May 2000, and again on 26 September 2000, as well as a decision dated 7 November 2001, extending the deadline for the filing of the appellant's brief, the appellant's brief was filed on 14 January 2002. In the introduction to the appellant's brief, the appellant claims that the additional evidence drawn from the Croatian centre archive and the proceedings in the Kordic trial, exonerates him from all charges and also claims that the Prosecution has withheld exculpatory evidence from -- submitted in the Kordic trial from disclosure in his case. He further argues that independent of the additional evidence, the Trial Chamber committed numerous errors of fact and law, warranting the reversal of the appellant's convictions. The appellant is seeking to have all of his convictions quashed. I will briefly summarise the grounds of appeal as follows: The first ground of appeal is that the appellant, Mr. Blaskic, did not have effective control of all HVO troops in Central Bosnia; that the HVO command structure was unorganised and ineffective; and that new evidence confirms the evidence presented at trial regarding the fragmented nature of the HVO command structure and his lack of effective control over the units operating in the Central Bosnia operative zone. The second ground of appeal is that no reasonable tribunal of fact could conclude that the appellant is responsible for crimes committed in the Vitez municipality. The appellant submits, as part of this ground, that no reasonable tribunal of fact could conclude that the appellant is responsible for crimes committed in Ahmici on 16 April 1993 and that he did not order the commission of any other crimes in the Vitez municipality. The third ground of appeal is that no reasonable tribunal of fact could conclude that the appellant is a responsible for crimes committed in the Busovaca municipality. As part of this ground, the appellant submits that he did not order the crimes in Loncari and Ocehnici. He's not liable under Article 7(3) for the crimes in these locations. And he is not responsible for the destruction of religious or educational property in Busovaca. The fourth ground of appeal is that no reasonable tribunal of fact could conclude that the appellant is responsible for crimes committed in Kiseljak municipality. The appellant submits that he did not order illegal attacks on civilians in April 1993, that he is not liable for the June 1993 campaign in Kiseljak, and that new evidence establishes that he did not have effective control over the HVO units in Kiseljak. The fifth ground of appeal is that the appellant is not guilty of detention crimes, that he did not order the cruel or inhuman treatment of detainees and that he has no command responsibility for the detention crimes. The sixth ground is that he was denied due process of law, namely, that the indictment against him was defective and cannot support his trial and conviction under Article 7(1) and 7(3), as a matter of law, and that the Prosecutor violated her disclosure obligations under Rule 68 and materially prejudiced the appellant's ability to conduct his defence. The seventh ground is that the Trial Chamber erred in finding the appellant guilty under Article 7. The Trial Chamber erred, the appellant says, when defining the specific elements of criminal responsibility under both Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) of the Statute. And by failing to draw a clear distinction between those two forms of liability. By doing so, the appellant states, the Trial Chamber provided the appellant with insufficient notice of the legal basis for his conviction, which in turn impedes his ability to appeal the judgement. The eighth ground is that the Trial Chamber erred in finding the appellant guilty of crimes against humanity, under Article 5. The ninth ground is that the Trial Chamber erred in its application of Article 2 of the Statute. The appellant submits that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that nationality does not determine protected person status within the meaning of Article 2, and that it erred in finding that Croatia and the Bosnian Republic were not co-belligerent states with normal diplomatic relations. The tenth and final ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred in its sentencing of the appellant. I would now like to remind the parties about the criteria applicable to errors of fact or law alleged on appeal. As the Appeal Chamber has pointed out on numerous occasions, an appeal is not an occasion for parties to re-plead their case. It is not a trial de novo. The general rule is that on appeal, the parties must limit their arguments to matters falling within the framework of Article 25 of the Statute, that is, errors on question of law invalidating the decision or errors of fact which have occasioned a miscarriage of justice. In a rare case, a party may raise an issue of general importance to the Tribunal's jurisprudence. An appellant alleging an error of fact must demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged and that this error has caused a miscarriage of justice. I will now like to outline the manner in which we will proceed for this hearing. As set out in the Scheduling Order issued by the Appeal Chamber on the 2nd of December, 2003, we will first hear the submissions of the Defence, which will have a total of four hours. Then the Prosecution will have in turn a total of four hours to submit its arguments in response. The floor will then go back to the Defence for its submissions in reply, which will take one hour, 45 minutes. Of course, parties are not requested to make use of all the time allocated to them. It also goes without saying that members of the Bench may put questions to the parties at the end of each pleading, should they deem it appropriate. At the conclusion of the hearing, the appellant himself may address briefly the Chamber if he so wishes. Breaks will take place as indicated in the Scheduling Order, or as otherwise appropriate. I would also like to remind the parties that if they have to refer to any testimony of a protected witness during their pleadings, they should use their pseudonyms and avoid mentioning any element that may reveal, directly or indirectly, the identity of the witness concerned. As the case may be, if it is absolutely necessary to mention elements that would disclose the identity, they should ask to go into closed session. I will now turn to the Defence for their submissions. Mr. Hayman, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, learned counsel. The appellant wishes to thank each of Your Honours for the long time and effort that has gone into this appeal. He recognises, as do we all, that this case is an arduous task with a voluminous record below, and with many complex questions. I would like to begin with a short roadmap of what the Defence expects to cover in our argument. First, I will address the Court with respect to the trial below, some observations; then the legal standard, because we do believe the legal standard governing these procedures should be modified somewhat as compared to other appeals; then I will cover different geographical areas, that of Ahmici, other locations in the Vitez municipality, the Busovaca municipality; Mr. Nobilo will address the Court with respect to the Kiseljak municipality; and I will address the Court with respect to a few remaining areas. There are, as the Court has outlined, a number of legal issues that are not as intensely factual as some of the ones I just outlined. We will not spend as much time on those legal issues in our argument. Four hours is enough time to cover some of our points but not all of our points in our, for example, very lengthy appellate brief. And after the final remarks by counsel tomorrow, I do expect the appellant to address you very briefly, and I hope he will be able to do so and that he feels well enough to be able to do so. He certainly hopes to. As Your Honour has indicated, I will go in and out of private session. I don't think there's anything I will be saying today that will require a closed session, although we may have to turn off the monitors when we're in private session, looking at at least one document that is under seal. I know it's customary for Your Honours to hold your questions until the end of counsel's statement. In my legal system, I'm used to being interrupted by the Court constantly, so I welcome that. If I say something that doesn't make sense and you'd like to take some of my time to ask a question, please do it. You are an audience of five and you are all that matters in this case at this point for the appellant. Your decisions and the information that you have to make the best decision that you can. I'm going to use certain visual aids this morning. They're going to all appear on the video monitors. And I believe that the correct button to see that material is the "computer evidence" button, at least that's the button we use here at our table. The material I'll be showing you consists of trial exhibits, of appellate material, of enlargements of trial transcripts, a couple of clips of actual testimony from the trial, video clips, and then a few charts which are not evidence but are argument of counsel, and those can be -- we can print those and provide them to lodge them as part of the record if the Court wishes. Of course we don't mean to suggest they're evidence. They're not evidence. They're mere aids in argument. First, the trial below. Our position continues to be that the trial below was infected. The most critical evidence to the case was not available at the time of the trial. The HVO War Archive was concealed. It was concealed by President Tudjman to protect himself and his political cronies. The appellant did not have access to the HVO War Archive during the trial. And indeed, he was convicted in part because he did not have access to this material. The Trial Chamber of course was frustrated that evidence was missing in the trial proceedings. And there is one point in the judgement where the Trial Chamber comments that although Blaskic claimed he ordered an investigation into the crimes at Ahmici by SIS, the absence of a SIS report casts doubt on his testimony that he actually ordered that investigation. May I just ask if some evidence or some material has appeared on the parties' and the Court's video screens? I know we had some trouble with the technology this morning. I see no troubled faces with respect to that question, Your Honour, so I will continue. We now have the report that the Trial Chamber commented was missing at trial and that cast doubt on appellant's veracity and on his testimony that he had ordered an investigation into the crimes in Ahmici, and indeed later on in my argument, when I'm addressing the failure-to-punish issue, I will give you a chronology that will include why this report fits in exactly the correct time period when it would have been prepared in response to appellant's orders. This is a SIS report of the crimes in Ahmici, prepared -- it's dated on 26 November 1993, and it names names and has at least a certain amount of particulars. The trial below was also infected because the intelligence services of both Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can you mention the exhibit, the number of the exhibit, when you refer to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I intend to in every such instance. This is Exhibit 1 to the first Rule 115 motion. The SIS report on Ahmici, the cover transmittal is dated 15 March, 1994. The actual underlying report which you see here is dated 26 November 1993. So both Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, the secret services of those countries, worked to prevent the Trial Chamber below from having access to the most relevant exculpatory evidence for appellant. On the Croatian side, the Security and Information Service, SIS, concealed the archive, as was later recounted in a report prepared by the Croatian authorities, and this is Exhibit 1 to the second Rule 115 motion, involving the difficulties and the lack of access that my co-counsel and I had to the War Archive and to the most critical reports, many of which dealt with the military police, the HVO military police, and which we were consistently not only denied access but told they didn't exist. In addition, authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina concealed critical BH army documents from the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber, at the Defence's request, issued two subpoenas to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on behalf of the Defence, one on the 28th of April, 1997, another on the 29th of April, 1998. As the Trial Chamber was informed, the responsive documents were not produced by the BH government, but we subsequently, after trial, learned that responsive documents did exist and had not been produced to us and to the Trial Chamber. And for examples of that, the Court can look at the fourth Rule 115 motion, Exhibits 12, 13, and 14, all BH army original documentation from the war, responsive to the subpoenas that the Trial Chamber issued that were not produced in a timely fashion, indeed weren't produced at all. We got these later on after the trial, through the Office of the Prosecutor. So we did not have the War Archive below. We had SIS and the BH army, the BH government, excuse me, with holding important records from the Trial Chamber, and unfortunately we had the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor also withholding a large amount of exculpatory material, in violation of Rule 68. And I don't mean by those comments to impugn our colleague Mr. Farrell. I'm not making a personal accusation against him. I'm not making a personal accusation against anyone. But what is absolutely clear is the Office of the Prosecutor, as a whole, had voluminous exculpatory material before and during the trial of appellant which, for whatever reason, was not produced, even though it should have been under Rule 68. How did this come to pass? Well, Colonel Blaskic and Mr. Kordic were indicted in a single indictment on the 10th of November, 1995. Colonel Blaskic came to The Hague voluntarily in April of 1996, wanted a trial, wanted to address this case, and his trial went forward. It went forward in June of 1997, alone, with no co-defendants. What then happened, after the Kordic proceedings came under way, is naturally the two trial teams vigorously pursued the best theory of their respective cases, but those theories diverged. Those theories diverged, and ultimately, the Prosecutor's office took different and indeed fundamentally inconsistent positions in the two cases. In the Blaskic case, they argued that a single military chain of command existed over all HVO units, without interference. And what you see now before you is from the trial transcript, page 24853. The Prosecutor's closing argument in the Blaskic case. And I will read it: "Your Honour, that the one person identified to kill civilians in this case, the one person identified as giving that order is Blaskic, nobody else. There's not one shred of evidence that anybody gave an order to kill from on high, and the only person that gave that order in the evidence in the record is Blaskic, the only one." Your Honours now know that the record has changed. That statement is no longer true. You can debate the weight of the evidence, but that statement is no longer true. If the Trial Chamber had had the evidence that Your Honours have, the Prosecutor could not have made that statement. What then evolved with respect to the Kordic and Blaskic Prosecutions was the use of witnesses in one that were not produced in the other. They were not only not used in the other, but the statements and exculpatory information, for example, that witnesses in Kordic provided - that is, exculpatory as to Blaskic - were not provided to Colonel Blaskic's Defence team. So in the Kordic case, the Prosecutor used Witness Watkins, BA3, by way of example, whereas in Blaskic, they used an EC monitor, for example, Mr. Baggesen, who in stark contrast to the testimony Your Honours heard last week, Mr. Baggesen testified that "the only one who had command over the military police was Mr. Blaskic himself." A very, very important piece of evidence in the Blaskic trial. We did not have all the evidence that Your Honours have seen, that you heard last week, that you've seen in the documents, to confront Mr. Baggesen with. I think if we had, he would have withdrawn his statement. He would have to. So this exculpatory evidence that was being used in the Kordic case was not provided to us, the Blaskic Defence. You saw the Watkins statement we got last week. We got it for the first time, despite the fact that it contained clearly exculpatory material. The same is true of the testimony of witnesses BA1, BA3, and BA5, which you have now heard for yourselves. And documents were not produced to us that were clearly Rule 68 materials. In our second Rule 115 motion we identify over 20 of these documents, and they are part of the record. Now, Rule 68 material has to be produced, regardless of whether there's a request for it. The Prosecutor may argue that these materials identifying the military -- direct military authority of Dario Kordic, Kordic's control over the Jokers, over criminal bands in Busovaca, they may say: This is not exculpatory because Blaskic and Kordic were two bodies, one mind, or they worked hand in glove. There, any evidence of the guilt of Kordic is also evidence of the guilt of Blaskic. What's wrong with that argument, which you may well hear? Well, one, the witnesses you have heard uniformly reject that argument. You heard that last week. They rejected two bodies, one brain, as a metaphor, or analogy, they rejected hand in glove, and I would direct you to the testimony, for example, of Philip Watkins and BA3. But furthermore, this argument that somehow any evidence against Kordic is also evidence against Blaskic, it is specious. It merely assumes away the existence of exculpatory material and it is also belied by the history and the well-articulated positions of the parties in this case. On the 26th of November, 1996, we filed -- appellant filed a motion to compel the production of Rule 68 material by the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor. We specifically demanded certain categories of documents in that motion. One category was, paragraph 3: "All evidence that individuals other than the accused and outside the formal HVO chain of command at any time exercised actual or de facto command and control over HVO activities alleged in the indictment to constitute a crime." We made it perfectly clear what was exculpatory material from the Defence perspective. This was a command responsibility case at the time, and we made it very clear what was needed. We also asked for information indicating that persons other than the accused exercised command or control over the detention of civilians. Your Honours heard testimony on that subject last week, testimony we should have had. In another paragraph which we weren't able to get imaged, we asked for: "All information tending to suggest that any persons other than the accused and military superiors and subordinates exercised on one or more occasions command and control over HVO military personnel or decisions." Namely, anyone outside the military chain of command exerting command or control over any military personnel or decisions. Paragraph 2(o), we also asked for the existence at any time material to the indictment of evidence of separate HVO and HDZ institutions, or separate chains of command and control over such institutions. We were specifically identifying the possibility that there were parallel, political, and military chains of command. The Prosecutor was ordered, in the Court's ruling on this motion, and this is before the Court now, to state to the Court whether the materials requested in our motion were in the Prosecutor's possession, whether they take a position contrary to the motion, i.e., that they don't contain exculpatory evidence, and if they do possess exculpatory evidence but there's some other reason why they shouldn't produce them due to confidentiality, et cetera, that they so advise the Court. That was not done. That was not done with respect to the materials that we have raised with this Court, we filed, attached to the second Rule 115 motion. It was not done with respect to Mr. Watkins' statement or the other statements that we discussed with Your Honours. For example, what did we learn when we got Philip Watkins' statement last week, thanks to the order that Your Honours entered? And this is from Exhibit H1, the statement that was produced last week. We learned in this portion of the statement, for example, that the Jokers, the very unit that was in Ahmici on the 16th of April and committed the crimes there, on other occasions had refused to accept Colonel Blaskic's authority and would only accept the authority of Dario Kordic. Mr. Watkins gave this statement to the Prosecutor on the 1st of June, 1996, about five months prior to our motion. This statement was taken about two months after the accused surrendered. It was taken for the purpose of his case. The investigators that took the statement were preparing for his trial, and yet this material was withheld from the Defence. We don't know what else is out there. We don't know what other Rule 68 material in the files of the Prosecutor's office, other witness statements, other notes, other information, is still there. To our knowledge no investigation has been conducted within the office of the Tribunal Prosecutor into these violations, and unfortunately it creates a situation now where the office as a whole is motivated, has an interest in defending its own conduct, which is a conflict of interest with pursuing the truth. But Your Honours have laboured long and hard to try and change the record and complete the record below, and for that we thank you. We have spent three years filing Rule 115 motions with you, and you patiently have reviewed them and made your decisions with respect to those motions. You have accepted 67 new items of documentary evidence, as well as the testimony of the witnesses we heard last week. So now the record on appeal is a mix of trial evidence and a very substantial body of new evidence that was not available to the Trial Chamber below. My point in summation is the cumulative effect of these defects in the trial below was there was a systematic bias in the documentary evidence available for the Trial Chamber. There was a systematic bias in the available witness testimony, and there was the advocacy of positions by the Office of the Prosecutor that were inconsistent with positions ultimately taken in other prosecutions. We do not fault the Trial Chamber for this. The Trial Chamber issued subpoenas to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber granted our Rule 68 motion and ordered the material produced. The Trial Chamber was misled. Now I'd like to turn to the legal framework. The Court has stated the normal standard of review in a case such as this, where there is some amount of Rule 115 evidence. The Kupreskic Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 75, recites the standard: "No reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached a conclusion of guilt based upon the evidence before the Trial Chamber, together with the additional evidence admitted during the appellate proceedings." That is the law of this Court at present. It's a deferential standard. Is it the correct standard here, given all that has gone on? You will be required to evaluate the credibility and trustworthiness of a significant volume of new evidence produced on appeal, both documentary and testimonial. There are no findings below by the Trial Chamber as to the credibility or the weight to be given to this new evidence. In that sense, you cannot defer to findings of the Trial Chamber as to such matters. Furthermore, there are direct clashes, many significant direct clashes, between the trial evidence and the new evidence that you have heard and received. For example, I've already talked about it and I will probably talk about it again. Did Colonel Blaskic have effective control over the military police? Mr. Baggesen said not only yes but that Blaskic was the only one who had effective control. You have now heard witnesses from every walk of life, civilians, military, et cetera, as well as the -- received the investigative product of the highest levels of the Croatian intelligence service, which absolutely refutes and belies that proposition. How are you to weigh and review that material under the "no reasonable tribunal of fact" standard? Similarly, with respect to the issue: Was there a BH army presence in Ahmici? Was there a BH army presence in Stari Vitez? That is, were there armed elements in those two localities at important times? You now have radically conflicting evidence in the new evidence on these points, which I will address later. Right now I'm addressing the procedural question of the legal standard. We propose that you must review this new mix of evidence de novo, first, as a practical matter. Because there are no findings, no credibility assessment, and indeed the Trial Chamber could not have assessed the value and credibility of the new evidence. You have to review that de novo. How do you review that de novo and yet defer to the Trial Chamber as to the old trial evidence? You must apply a uniform standard to the evidence, and that standard must be de novo. There's another reason that that must be the standard. Where a significant portion of the new evidence on key matters was withheld from the Trial Chamber, in violation of Rule 68, international standards of due process of law require either a new trial or, at a minimum, de novo review. In the United Kingdom, the courts have uniformly that he would once it is determined on appeal that the new evidence renders the verdict unsafe, the conviction must be quashed and either an acquittal or a new trial granted. Of course, at the new trial, all evidence is tested under a proof beyond reasonable doubt standard. This is set forth, for example, in the McNamee case, 1998 C.A., 17 December 1998. In the United States, the standard is similar, under Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963). Reversal is required when the new evidence impacts or undermines evidence that was central to the case. Here, the Prosecutor's suppression of evidence precluded appellant's ability to effectively prepare his case, it distorted the evidentiary record presented to the Trial Chamber and denied the appellant a fair trial under the principles of this Tribunal. Applying the "no reasonable tribunal of fact" standard would reward Rule 68 violations by permitting the Prosecutor to prevail on a lower standard of proof on appeal than she would have faced at trial had all the evidence that should have been produced been produced. That would be a miscarriage of justice to incentivise [sic] Prosecutors in this way. And I'm not suggesting that they would respond to that incentive. But that just cannot be. That cannot be the law of this Tribunal, that that kind of conduct results in a higher standard, a higher hurdle for an appellant in this situation. We also submit that in weighing the evidence, should you not order a new trial, you are going to be confronted with situations where there are grey areas, there are unknowns, where you heard from a witness and you didn't hear from a trial witness, it will be difficult to weigh and compare that evidence. It follows, we believe, from the "proof beyond a reasonable doubt" standard, and from the fact that you should be reviewing this material de novo, that uncertainties and doubts in those comparisons must be drawn in favour of the appellant and we also believe this is true due to the fact if he doesn't receive a new trial, that he will never have an appeal from Your Honours' decision. And every developed system of law provides for an appeal from the finder of fact. He will not have an appeal from Your Honours' decision. He accepts that. We're not complaining. But because there will be no appeal, doubts should be drawn in his favour, not against him. There are a couple of themes that I'd like to touch upon. I'm moving now out of the legal standard area, and I'd like to touch on a couple of themes before I address the crimes in Ahmici. One of the themes from the judgement that I've already alluded to is that guilt was inferred in certain respects from a lack of evidence available before the Trial Chamber. The failure of the appellant to produce the SIS report on the crimes in Ahmici is the leading example, and now you have it. Now you have that document. We also have a much more complete set of the reports, of the orders issued by appellant at the critical time, on the 15th of April and early in the morning on the 16th of April. During the trial, we did not have Prosecutor's rebuttal Exhibit PA12. This is an order to the military police with respect to their duties to secure and defend the Vitez-Busovaca road and repel any enemy attack. This document came from the Croatian archives. And as you're reviewing the evidence in your deliberations, any document you see in the upper right-hand corner, this stamp, this round stamp, that means it came from the archives, and indeed this is a document that the Prosecutor submitted, purportedly in rebuttal. We thank him for doing so. It clarifies exactly what orders were given to the military police. It's an exculpatory document, and now you have it. A second theme that I'd like to comment upon is the concentration of the crimes found by the Trial Chamber in certain very limited time periods. If you read the indictment, the indictment talks about crimes from 1992 to 1994, continuous, ongoing, widespread. If you compare that with the judgement, the judgement found basically all of the crimes, at least the vast majority, on literally a few limited days, almost all in the spring of 1993. So in Vitez, they found crimes on the 16th, the 18th of April; in Kiseljak, 18th of April; Busovaca, 17th to 19th of April; Kiseljak, 12th of June; and then finally the Grbavica battle on the 7th of September, 1993. My point is: As you examine that material and you examine the efforts of the appellant to build a military organisation where discipline was respected, where orders were respected, where criminal conduct was not condoned, you see over the time line that when war broke out in April, you had crimes. And as these efforts to organise the HVO and create a more disciplined force, that those efforts bore fruit. And you can see that when you look these data points, these points in time when the Trial Chamber found crimes were committed. Now I'd like to go to the Ahmici crimes. What is Ahmici to this case? It was indisputably the centrepiece of the Prosecution before the Trial Chamber. More recently, on the 21st of November of last year, our colleague said in his argument before Your Honours, and I quote: "This case is not about Ahmici." Why are they moving away from Ahmici as the centrepiece of their case? Well, they're moving away from it because their evidence has crumbled and has been utterly refuted by the new evidence. Ahmici is the reason, we submit, that appellant was indicted; it's the reason this case became the subject of political intrigue in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina; it's the reason he was convicted; and it's the reason that he was given a sentence that exceeds his likely natural life. Having used Ahmici to secure this sentence, the Prosecutor cannot now claim that Ahmici is a mere footnote to this case. It is the heart and soul of their case. Where does the story of Ahmici begin? At the trial below, the story began in Ahmici, it began in Vitez, it began in the Hotel Vitez. We now know, based on the new evidence, the story of Ahmici begins in Busovaca in 1992 and in January of 1993. How do we know that? We know from this SIS report in the fall of 1992, Exhibit 102 to the first Rule 115 motion, that in 1992, Anto Sliskovic was forming his own special unit, a special unit of individuals. And this is later in the same report, page 2, the fourth bullet: "That in 1992 were starting to terrorise the Muslim population in Busovaca so as to provoke interethnic conflict and create tension between Croats and Muslims." As an aside, Your Honours, as professional Judges, you know how to evaluate evidence, but I point out: This report was written in 1992. It's from the archive, if I'm not mistaken. There's no issue as to its authenticity. There's no claim that in 1992 someone was creating information to mislead Your Honours or mislead this Court. This kind of evidence is the best evidence, created before people had motives to distort or misrepresent the evidence. And then, moving into January of 1993, there's now voluminous evidence establishing that that conflict was started by Kordic and Sliskovic to create tension and terrorise the Muslim population. This is a portion of Exhibit 14 to the fourth Rule 115 motion, noting that these -- this special unit, the prime mover is Anto Sliskovic, with whom there are eight other soldiers, extremists, alongside Sliskovic are Vlado Cosic and Zarko Milic, supported by Dario Kordic. And this information is not limited to information developed by SIS. This is Exhibit D591, from the 28th of April, 1993. It's an ECMM report, noting that: "Mr. Kordic, located in Busovaca, is the man -- the main responsible identified by all agencies of the troubles in Busovaca two months before." Namely, in the January/February time frame. And then it goes on to talk about Kordic controlling military HVO forces. There are other SIS reports. Again, this SIS report, Exhibit 8 to the first Rule 115 motion, again dated 18 February 1993, before war broke out in the Vitez municipality, noting the formation of Kordic's and Kostroman's special private police, headed by Sliskovic, which now has grown to 30 or 40 members. They're criminals, and they're given the dirtiest assignments, such as murder, robbery et cetera, called a squadron of death. The witness testimony that Your Honours have now heard is the same. Witness BA4, a lifelong resident of Busovaca, testified before Your Honours that there was only one person in charge of everything that happened then, May 1992, and that happened later on. It was just one, and one person only: Dario Kordic, with his followers. That was from the transcript of our hearing around page 485. I don't have a precise cite. On page 485 of the transcript that witness went on to describe it was following his orders, Sliskovic, that all the looting and nightmares occurred by his followers, his subjects, who were the Jokers in the police and in the military police. Thus, SIS, ECMM, and there was a BH army exhibit in there. I'm sorry if I misidentified it. Let's look. Let's go back to Exhibit 14, to the fourth Rule 115 motion. This passage is from a BH army report dated 26 January 1993. My apologies for misstating the source of that material. Thus SIS, the BH army, the European Monitoring Mission, all found that Kordic and Sliskovic ordered crimes of terror, directed crimes of terror against Muslims in Busovaca before January 1993, in January 1993, and that they included the use of the Jokers and the HVO military police in those clandestine criminal acts. That is where the story of Ahmici begins. You are now, because of the new evidence, in a position to contrast the extremist and criminal purposes of those I've just been discussing with Colonel Blaskic's attitude and motives. And for this, I need to briefly go into private session and to turn off the monitor for the gallery. I will only need a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Following up on that point: In the record, and I don't have them to show to Your Honours, but in the record, there are a series of about eight orders, from February of 1993, co-signed by Colonel Blaskic and General Hadzihasanovic, or other BH army representatives, implementing a number of these joint command type orders -- we need to make sure that what we just had isn't up on the monitor. I don't think it is. I think it's a picture instead. There are volumes, if you will, of material, documentary material, supporting the accused's efforts -- If it's on the monitor -- well, it's not on the public monitor. I can see it's not on the monitor out there. But maybe we -- tell you what, I'll go to something else, to eliminate any possibility that it's on the screen. I'm just going back to an exhibit we've already discussed, for witness security purposes. So there are voluminous joint commission, joint command documents substantiating the testimony we just looked at. And fundamentally, when you ask the question: What were Blaskic's motives? What was he trying to do? What did he want? The Court knows -- the Court now knows that what happened after Ahmici was -- of course, it evoked a tremendous backlash from the BH army. The HVO was outnumbered 10 to 1 or 7 to 1 in the Lasva Valley, and this is the statement of Philip Watkins. What happened? What happened after Ahmici? He describes it as this HVO military failure prompted a strong BH army reaction and led to direct military confrontation with the HVO. The HVO suffered military defeats in the Lasva and other valleys, and a further consequence was the isolation of the Croat communities into defensive pockets. The HVO was in a horrible military situation in the Lasva Valley, encircled in these pockets. The last thing that Colonel Blaskic, as the military commander, wanted was to have the 3rd Corps and the other BH army corps coming at him from all directions in these tiny pockets. What happened in Ahmici was a military disaster in terms of what Colonel Blaskic wanted. And the reason, how can we harmonise that? It wasn't conceptualised as a military action. It was terror. It was conceptualised, as Your Honours now know, as an act of terror to try and to drive Muslims out of the region and that was the last thing that Colonel Blaskic wanted. So that's the backdrop. That's where the story begins. What actually happened in Ahmici? You now have before you evidence that allows you to make a fresh assessment of whether the appellant bears criminal culpability for the Ahmici massacre. Please remember, on the 27th or so of January, the Vitez-Busovaca pocket had been cut off from the Kiseljak pocket. That was triggered by the night-time clandestine terror acts of the -- Sliskovic and his group around the 20th and 21st of January. That triggered a military response. Kiseljak is cut off by the 27th of January, a fact that was not unnoticed in the Hotel Vitez. On the 15th of April, the HVO brigade commander, Commander Totic, is kidnapped and his four bodyguards are shot dead outside Zenica. You heard last week that by mid-April, both the HVO and the BH army were on heightened alert for possible conflict. And you saw, from Exhibit D193, that the HVO was indeed wary of an escalation. And while D193 is significant, what is more significant is the logic that the most vulnerable point for the Vitez-Busovaca pocket was the narrowest point and the point that was adjacent to the largest Muslim populations, and that was Ahmici on the north and then the corresponding portions of the terrain to the south. And that is what D193 was pointing out, is that this is our most vulnerable point in terms of having the Vitez-Busovaca pocket cut in two. You heard testimony last week that this type of manoeuvre would be logical to anyone with even rudimentary military training. In this context, you have the three key orders issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 15th of April, in the early morning of the 16th of April. The first is the preparatory order, D267, which was issued after the report that Totic had been kidnapped and that terrorist attacks, if you will, against HVO commanders were escalating. Then D269 was issued, an order to the HVO Vitez Brigade and to the Tvrtko unit, and the operative word is "blockade." This was an order to blockade BH army forces in Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska, the following morning at 5.30 a.m. And then now you have Exhibit PA12, a rebuttal exhibit from the Prosecutor, which is the corresponding order to the 4th Battalion of the military police, telling them to block approaches to the road. Were these orders implemented? Were they followed? No, they were not. On the afternoon of the 15th of April, the first preparatory order, D267, was completed. And the evidence is that Pasko Ljubicic set in motion the gathering of his military police unit at the Bungalow later that evening. But that afternoon, the unit was not told that a massacre would be committed in Ahmici. That did not occur until the early morning of the 16th of April. Why? What happened in the intervening time? This is Exhibit 1 from the second Rule 115 motion, a report by the Ministry of the Interior in Croatia, describing a meeting later on that night, composed of Dario Kordic, Ignac Kostroman, Sliskovic, Ljubicic, Vlado Cosic, and others, and at that meeting, the directive to burn Ahmici and to kill men of military age was given. And I think I need a short private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So this is Exhibit 4 to the first Rule 115 motion. HIS and SIS concluded that Kordic and Kostroman were responsible for the crime. Just to elaborate, it is important, I think, to assess what access did SIS and HIS have to the relevant information? They had access to people within SIS, they had access to people within the military police, they had access to the wounded that had been evacuated to Split and other cities in Croatia, they had access to all the documentary evidence, and this is what they concluded. Regrettably, they had access to far more information and relevant evidence on this question than any of us ever will, and this is what they concluded, at a time when there was no motive to fabricate or cover up. Their motive was to give accurate information to their political leader, Franjo Tudjman, and, indeed, identifying the political leadership in Central Bosnia, that was a smear on President Tudjman. It was against his interest to be told members of your political party, your political representatives in Central Bosnia are responsible for these crimes. It was not what Franjo Tudjman wanted to hear, and that lends additional credibility to these findings. The next question, having covered the orders: Did Colonel Blaskic learn of the Ahmici crimes on the 16th of April? What was he told? Well, we know that he got a written report, which is Exhibit D280. He got a report late in the day on the 16th of April, from Pasko Ljubicic. This was in response to his request. And this report concealed the fact that a massacre had been committed in Ahmici. Blaskic had no basis upon which to conclude that crimes were being or had been committed in Ahmici on the 16th of April. He was in the basement of the Hotel Vitez. There was a widespread conflict throughout the municipality. The evidence is not controverted that from the Hotel Vitez or from Vitez, for that matter, one could not discern the difference between combat activities and a crime, based on smoke and noise some distance away in Ahmici. That being the case, at the trial below, the Prosecutor went to great lengths to try and prove that there was no armed resistance in Ahmici. There were no BH army or other armed Muslim forces there. And they presented Western observer evidence to that effect, that they toured Ahmici later and they saw no weapons, no other evidence that there had been an armed resistance. And the Trial Chamber accepted that testimony and it's recounted in the judgement at paragraphs 407 to 410. We agree that there were no units of the 3rd Corps in Ahmici but there was a Territorial Defence unit of some 30 to 35 men, with weaponry, and Your Honours heard that testimony last week from an official who was in a position to know, BA5. That fact can no longer be disputed. Furthermore, the fact that there was a military conflict on the 16th of April, involving TO forces at the school in Ahmici, can no longer be disputed, based on testimony Your Honours heard. Furthermore, we have new evidence from the BH army itself that on the 16th of April, forces were ordered to go to Ahmici. And this is Exhibit 12 to the fourth Rule 115 motion, in which the 3rd Corps, on the 16th of April, orders a company from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade to go to Ahmici to organise and carry out a march and arrive there to assist our forces in the defence and organise the defence. This is one of the orders that we should have gotten when the subpoena was issued to BH and that we only got much later, after the trial. We do not claim -- the Defence has never claimed that there was a particular military justification to attack this TO unit in Ahmici. That is not our thesis. We don't have to claim that. Colonel Blaskic did not order an attack on Ahmici. But what is critical is that there was a military justification to defending the Vitez-Busovaca road and that once there was a conflict in Ahmici, it was absolutely normal for Colonel Blaskic to believe that it was a military conflict, because there were TO units in these villages, including Ahmici. Did the British Battalion inform Colonel Blaskic that there were crimes in Ahmici on the 16th? They did not. They went to Ahmici in their Warriors and they didn't observe any massacre or comparable activity. The BH army was not aware of any crimes on the 16th. And the point here is that failure to prevent liability requires that the accused know that there's a crime ongoing and have the opportunity to do something about it and stop it, and here there can be no liability for failing to prevent or stop a crime of which the accused did not have knowledge. So these are the events, these are what actually happened on the 15th and 16th of April. The new evidence confirms this. Apart from the primary evidence, the witnesses you've heard, the new primary documents, the SIS and HIS investigations confirm these very events. And these were important investigations. The Ahmici massacre was headline news on CNN on April 22nd, 1993. It caused an international outcry. It caused a huge embarrassment for the Bosnian-Croat community, and indeed for Franjo Tudjman, then-president of Croatia. The investigations that were done for him were serious. It was a serious issue, and all the information that you see in this regard, they are not propaganda reports; they're internal, secret confidential reports for the eyes of the Croatian president and other intelligence officials in Mostar and in Croatia. There's one document now under seal, Your Honour, that I need to have a private session to discuss, and we'll need to make sure that the document, when I show it, doesn't go up on the public screen. I think, in reality, it may not -- it may no longer need to be under seal, but it's still under seal and so I have to treat it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: By contrast, let us look at Exhibit 13 to the first Rule 115 motion. This is a SIS report concerning Ahmici, prepared on June 8th. This is 20 days after the report we just looked at. A mere 20 days later, we have a SIS report which says what it says. It identifies the military police. It identifies the Jokers. It identifies the Bungalow as their location. And while it appears to, in part, be based on the statement of one Zoran Krista, which we know and Your Honours know is part false, part true. This individual is saying: Well, we did these things only after we were provoked, or whatever. But still, the report goes on to say that everyone in sight was killed, and names are identified, and the unit is identified. So you can contrast that with the other evidence and understand that this was prepared by the Department of Defence. This is a different document, not prepared by the author of the other document, which tells you that at this point in time, you have different lines within that organisation conducting themselves very, very differently. Colonel Blaskic did not receive this report. He never got any of the SIS or HIS reports, and you can look at all the cover pages and transmittals showing they were not for him. They were for SIS and HIS in Mostar and for President Tudjman in Zagreb. The same is true if you look at the first exhibit to the first Rule 115 motion, the November 26 SIS report. This is the second page. The judgement, as I've recounted, and this is paragraph 493 of the judgement, found that the accused has not shown that he made any sustained efforts to recover the report before appearing before the Tribunal. This is the report we're discussing, the first exhibit to the first Rule 115 motion: "Although that report was the item of evidence most likely to exonerate him, consequently these findings cast doubt on the very existence of such a report." And indeed, this is the report that the Trial Chamber so desperately wanted to see, and if you look at the guts of that report, prepared on the 26th of November, you can see that SIS has developed considerably more information by now and the report not only identifies the Jokers; it identifies the command of the Jokers, Vlado Cosic, and Pasko Ljubicic, and identifies other individuals involved in the crimes within the Jokers unit and Cicko, who was added to the force that attacked Ahmici on the 16th of April. And I've already told you that a few months later, on 17 February, in the 1994 HIS report, prepared for President Tudjman, the Croatian Intelligence Service reported that Dario Kordic and Ignac Kostroman are responsible for the crime in Ahmici. Now I'd like to turn to the judgement and what the judgement found concerning Ahmici, and what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I think we should approach a break. I don't know whether before turning to the judgement this is an appropriate moment to break or not. It depends on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I'm right at a transition point, so this would be a logical point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So let's break now for half an hour, according to our schedule, and we'll reconvene at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. We will now resume. Mr. Hayman, you may continue your pleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was turning from a recounting of the events in Ahmici to what did the Trial Chamber find regarding Ahmici, and how might Your Honours go about an analysing those findings in light of the new evidence. The starting point was set out in 437 of the judgement, which found that the order, D269, was an order to attack. It found that on the face of the order, it was an order to attack. It did not find that the order was code language for an attack or a wink and a nod order for an attack. It found within the four corners of the document, it was an order to attack the village of Ahmici. That is contrary, Your Honours, to the new evidence. An indeed, there's an absence of evidence at trial that this was an order to attack. The Prosecutor chose at trial not to bring a military expert, or anyone with military training, to the trial, and ask them whether D269 was a legal order or an order to attack a civilian population and thus an illegal order. They consciously did not do that. That was not part of their evidence. And so it is an unusual situation that now we find ourselves with this statement in the judgement, nonetheless, and very fortunate that we've had an opportunity to augment the record for Your Honours, because now Your Honours have had more of an advocacy proceeding, if you will, with respect to this key pivotal issue. I also note, I'm greatly looking forward to hearing what my learned colleagues have to say about this order. I note last week they did not question any of the witnesses who testified about the legality of these orders, such as BA1, or BA3. They did not cross-examine them at all as to the legality and proprietariness [sic] of D269 or D267 or PA12. In light of the new evidence, I think that these orders -- the proper interpretation of these orders is pretty clear. First of all, this again is D269, with the addressee box blown up. These are the units to whom this order was addressed. This was not an order to the military police. The Trial Chamber found that this was an order to the military police to attack the civilian population of Ahmici. So the first important point is: It was not an order to the military police, period, full stop. Now, secondly, D269 is not an order to attack. It is a defensive order written in standard military terminology, which you heard last week was perfectly clear on the face of the document. At this point, with the new evidence, we submit, even under a "reasonable tribunal of fact" standard, that no such tribunal could conclude either that D269 was an order to the military police or that it was an order to attack or that it was an order to attack civilians. All three of those premises are in error. And as Your Honours will see, and as my colleague has pointed out, if you look at the left-hand side of this order, which I'm afraid I can't move this box right now, but this is an order to the Vitez Brigade and the Tvrtko unit to block Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska, which are to the south and on the other side of the communication line from Ahmici. It's a different geographic area. So different units, different geographic area, different mission, et cetera. So what did the -- how did the Trial Chamber get there? What is it that they found in order to come to the conclusion that they came? They said there were three types of forces in Ahmici: The Domobrani, or Home Guard, the military police, and the Vitez Brigade. The evidence is very clear that the military police were in Ahmici. The evidence is, however, that neither the home guard nor the Vitez Brigade participated in the attack on Ahmici. The Domobrani is something like a system of reserves, and so people are signed up for it. And the Trial Chamber found that because the reserves were within the military chain -- the military hierarchy, that they must have participated and Blaskic must have ordered them to attack civilians. There are no orders to the Domobrani in connection with Ahmici, much less any orders to attack civilians. With respect to the military police, we absolutely agree; they were in Ahmici. Where we differ with the Trial Chamber is that the appellant had neither -- did not have effective control over the Jokers, and he certainly did not have sole effective control, as the Trial Chamber found, via the Baggesen testimony. You'll recall last week Mr. Watkins testified that it was the conventional wisdom and belief within the ECMM that the Jokers were under the effective control of Dario Kordic, transcript appellate hearing 294. And now I need a very brief private session. I apologise. This is an area where I'm going to have to jump back and forth a couple of times, and we might as well get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We are in open session. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We submit at base, however, that the issue with respect to Ahmici of whether at some theoretical level Colonel Blaskic had effective control over the Jokers, it's really moot, because we now have direct evidence as to who ordered the crime. We don't have to make guesstimates based on: There's only one chain of command and therefore if they're under Blaskic's chain of command, Blaskic must have ordered the crime. You have direct evidence that the crime was committed -- was ordered, excuse me, by someone else, and you have extensive evidence concerning the ability and the power of that other authority, to use the Jokers, to order them into combat, and to direct them to commit criminal activity against Muslim civilians. You also have the SIS and HIS reports, which inculpate Kordic, Sliskovic, Ljubicic, and Cosic for the massacre and exonerate Blaskic. And I note in that regard that at the time these reports were written, President Tudjman had absolute power in Croatia. His son, Miroslav Tudjman, was the head of the Croatian Intelligence Service, HIS, or HIS. So some of the reports that you have are reports from the son to the absolute political authority in Croatia, delivering bad news, news that had to be in the view of those preparing these reports, absolutely rock solid. What about the Trial Chamber's reliance on Mr. Baggesen's testimony? If you look at his testimony, he was too an ECMM monitor. He was in Central Bosnia for about two months and 19 days. He did not speak the language. And when giving his opinion that only Colonel Blaskic could control the military police, he gave one example, and only one example, to support his opinion. And his example was that when he was arrested, along with other individuals, by the military police, that it was only Colonel Blaskic that could free the captives from the military police. And now I must go back into private session to elaborate, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So as we are discussing, the Trial Chamber found that the Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici on the 16th. Now we know that is not correct. In part, the Trial Chamber relied on Exhibit D269, as an order to attack Ahmici. And it is true D269 is directed to the Vitez Brigade, but of course it not only does not order the Vitez Brigade into Ahmici, it orders them to go somewhere else. So part of the underlying error here, Your Honours, was that this order was misunderstood. When properly understood it tends to prove the contrary proposition to what the Trial Chamber found. And further, we know, because the Croatian Intelligence Service investigated this matter, that they found and they wrote in a report to Franjo Tudjman, on 21 March 1994 - and this is the 14th exhibit to the first Rule 115 motion - specifically that the attack on Ahmici was carried out by the Jokers, and then the individuals involved in a command position are named. And then later on down the page, and this is page 2, this secret intelligence report states: "It can be said with certainty that Mario Cerkez was not involved in the massacre in the village of Ahmici and that he had no influence on these events." Mario Cerkez, of course, was the Vitez Brigade commander. This is a reference to the Vitez Brigade. Now, in the appeal proceedings, it's been quite interesting. The Prosecutor has largely abandoned the evidence cited by the Trial Chamber in support of its position and now the Prosecutor has moved on to try and develop new evidence to support the findings of the Trial Chamber below. And this is Exhibit PA6, and it is one of the leading pieces of new evidence that the Prosecutor is attempting to rely upon. Basically, what they have argued in their papers is the Vitez Brigade had to be in Ahmici because on the 16th of April - and this is a -- this is PA6 - the Vitez Brigade wrote a report to the operative zone, in which it said: "Our forces are advancing on Donja Veceriska and in Ahmici," while in other villages there's a truce and so forth. And the Prosecutor has argued in its briefs this shows the Vitez Brigade was in Ahmici. Not so fast. Not so fast. If you look at this report, you'll see at the top, and we've blown it up, it's a report on the situation in the area of responsibility. It's not a report on the activities of the Vitez Brigade. It's a report on the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade, which is the Vitez municipality. And then if you look down at the lower portion that we've enlarged, it doesn't refer to the Vitez Brigade specifically. It says "our forces," referring to Croatian forces. And then it does speak to Donja Veceriska, which is one of the locations where is the Vitez Brigade was directed to be on the morning of the 16th. But the other places are not. We know that the Vitez Brigade was not in Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, and I'm not sure exactly where Vrhovine is any more, so many years have passed in this case. But these are references to other Croatian forces in other locations, in the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade, but the Vitez Brigade was not everywhere, in all these places at this time, and the report doesn't indicate anything of the sort. Indeed, if we look at some of the other new evidence, such as the 14th exhibit to the second Rule 115 motion, the war diary, the war diary makes clear that at 9.00, orders were given to the Vitez Brigade commander, Mario Cerkez, to block the shooting on the fire station building in Vitez. And that's consistent with the orders given in D269 as to where the Vitez Brigade was supposed to be on the morning of the 16th. There are no entries in the war diary inconsistent with these propositions that the Vitez Brigade was in Vitez, Kruscica, Donja Veceriska, et cetera. They were not in Ahmici. And finally, I note, although we do not cite to any other decisions of this Tribunal with respect to factual findings, and I'm not citing here to the Kupreskic appeals judgement as a matter of precedent. I'm simply noting that their logic is rather clear and, I think, powerful, that "It's difficult to accept" - and this is at paragraph 213, I believe - "It is difficult to accept the suggestion that the Vitez Brigade was deployed to Ahmici to participate in the attack in the early morning of 16 April 1993 as a unit. The commander of the Vitez Brigade had received instructions to engage in military activities in other villages in the Vitez area at the relevant time." So to return to the judgement and the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 467, the judgement found, and I quote: "The planned nature and, in particular, the fact that all these units acted in a perfectly coordinated manner presupposes in fact that these troops were responding to a single command, which accordingly could only be superior to the commander of each of these units." What is the Trial Chamber talking about here? They're talking about having found that there were three different units in Ahmici - the military police, the Vitez Brigade, and the Domobrani - that therefore, because the activity was coordinated, that it had to have been commanded at a level above the Vitez Brigade, above the military police, and above the Home Guard. Well, whether that's true or false, whether the activity, killing civilians and burning houses, whether that was coordinated or not, the fact is, the underlying supposition that there were three units in Ahmici is wrong. The military police were in Ahmici. There was no supra-coordination required. The coordination happened on the morning of the 16th, when the orders to kill and to burn, to kill civilians and torch the village were given. Those were the coordinating orders, and they have nothing to do with Colonel Blaskic and they had nothing to do with the logic set forth in paragraph 467 of the judgement. So this finding, this finding is simply irrelevant, because you now know, I submit, based on the new evidence, there was one unit in Ahmici. Furthermore, because you have direct evidence as to who ordered the crimes in Ahmici, we submit you don't have to undertake this type of abstract analytical reasoning. You should go -- you should look first to the direct evidence. Now, we also have given you extensive evidence that Colonel Blaskic did not have effective control over the Jokers, and indeed that other authorities exercised direct control over the Jokers and used the Jokers for criminal purposes. But my point is, the logical nexus, that because this activity was organised and because there was a single command and therefore Blaskic had to order the crimes, that logical nexus is broken; it does not exist any more, in light of the new evidence. Finally, the Trial Chamber did cite elsewhere that because some form of mortars or artillery were used prior to the actual attack on civilians in Ahmici, that that indicated some high level of planning to the operation. That we believe is not true, and that was made clear last week. Philip Watkins testified in the hearing last week at 297 that "Artillery, followed by an infantry attack, is standard military practice. It would not mean that you -- because of seeing that combination, you could say: Ah, this is the obvious work of a particular commander." Before I leave Ahmici, before I leave the events and the conviction for failure to prevent, I would like to draw your attention to one other source of valuable information on this issue, and that is Colonel Blaskic's state of mind when he learned there had been a massacre. How did he react? Not what was written by the propaganda department six months later in a magazine. How did he react, according to percipient witnesses, when he was told there was a massacre? You have two important pieces of evidence on that question. First, the testimony of Colonel Stuart, who was the commander of BritBat, and he testified that when confronted with evidence of the massacre on April 22nd, he was sure that Blaskic was horrified. Those are his words: Horrified. And that's in the record below. It's recounted in our brief. Secondly, there was a press conference on April 27th, 1993, in the Lasva Valley. It was covered by local television. And I put it to you, Colonel Blaskic was there. Did he use this press conference to put out propaganda to suggest a cover story, or did he do something else. Well, fortunately there was a witness at this press conference, a man who testified at trial, a former member of parliament in the United Kingdom, a former war correspondent, Martin Bell, and this is what Bell saw at that press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We need sound. Perhaps the technical booth can assist us in how we can hear the testimony. It's an interesting picture, but it's not that interesting. We really need the sound. Hearing no response -- well, if we unplug my laptop and turn up the volume, Your Honours can hear it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My only thing that concerns me is once we unplug, what happens when we re-plug?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I'm told the technician is on his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We'll line this up, and maybe we can do it with the other computer. Of course, timing the image with the sound using two different computers could be tricky, but we'll come back to this point as soon as the technical assistance is there. So in one way or another, I'm going to play for you what Martin Bell saw at this press conference, and it's very important. And after you've heard that, I think that you will understand what Colonel Blaskic testified at trial, at reporter's transcript 20136, which, with respect to the Danas interview, he said that there was no interview, there was no correspondent that came to Central Bosnia. Apparently, questions were faxed to the command. The Information and Propaganda Department, IPD, filled out answers to the questions, and they were mailed out, or whatever, to the journalist, and Colonel Blaskic never authorised the text of the interview. You also heard Mr. Watkins testify last week that that propaganda piece, those words did not sound, did not convey to him as Blaskic's words, and they were entirely out of character. But I think once you hear what happened at the press conference, you'll be satisfied of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We're going to try again. So here we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. Did then Colonel Blaskic addressed the subject of the massacre in Ahmici at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I made some notes at the time which I, with the agreement of the Court, will read. He said he was horrified. He was going to do something about it, that "... a commission is being set up to investigate the atrocities. Whoever did it did it in an organised, systematic way. It was an organised group of people operating to a plan and, therefore, controlled by someone. The culprits must be identified and brought to justice." And Colonel Blaskic said he was appalled."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I don't know if the -- Your Honour, perhaps we can play it again for the court reporter later, if that's acceptable. It looks like she missed some pieces because it was difficult to hear because of the makeshift audio. But in substance, what Martin Bell said was that Colonel Blaskic, he laid down the gauntlet. He said it was a shocking crime, that it was organised, there were culprits, and they must be found, and he said that on local television in the Lasva Valley. He laid down the gauntlet to send that message to the Bosnian Croat community in the Lasva Valley. And that is utterly inconsistent with the attempt of the Prosecutor to paint Blaskic as someone who was making excuses and trying to promulgate a cover story with respect to Ahmici. Now, that exhausts the bases of liability for the attack on Ahmici that are in the Trial Chamber's judgement. There are no other bases and we submit that that conviction should not be allowed to stand. What about failure to punish, which has two components: Failure to prevent and failure to punish. That requires separate treatment. Initially, I note that a conviction for both ordering a crime and failing to prevent it is internally inconsistent. And that's a problem we had at trial. We never knew where the Prosecution was going, because we were simultaneously having to defend: Did he order it? Did he fail to prevent it? And they never committed. They never made a commitment as to those inconsistent theories, despite the fact, as I'll recite later, the Trial Chamber found that was a defect in the indictment and that the Prosecution would bear full weight, the full consequences, if they failed to cure that defect. So nonetheless, we tried to defend on all fronts, as we had to, and with respect to failure to prevent, I've largely addressed that. On the morning of the 16th, Blaskic was in the basement of the hotel. He did not have information that a crime was in progress. And that was largely based, the Trial Chamber found, on the testimony from Colonel Stuart, at reporter's transcript 23743, that at 10.00 a.m. on the 16th, Stuart went to the Hotel Vitez and was not able to see Blaskic. Well, now that we have the war diary, we know what happened at the Hotel Vitez that morning, when Colonel Stuart went to try and find Blaskic. Colonel Stuart was there. He was there ten minutes early, at 10 to 10.00, and he spoke to another member of the staff, Marko Prskalo but there's no indication that he was taken into the command centre, the basement where they were, rather he had some kind of an exchange with Prskalo, and they had a discussion. What was Blaskic doing at 9.50 a.m.? We also know that from the war diary, and that is the 14th exhibit to the Rule 115 motion, that first passage was page 73, paragraph 3. This is a passage at page 72, the last paragraph. At 9.50 a.m., Blaskic was there. This is a war diary of what was happening in the command post, and he was on the phone with another member of the command staff, someone called Batinic. At 10.00, Colonel Blaskic had another call, so he went from one call to the next, and at 10.00, the call was with the commander of the Kiseljak Brigade. So it is true that Colonel Stuart didn't have a conversation, a face-to-face with Colonel Blaskic, and the Trial Chamber inferred from that Blaskic must not have been at the hotel. He was at the hotel but he was tied up. They were in the middle of firefights all across the Vitez municipality. So Blaskic was there, he was in the basement, he was there all day, and if there's anything inconsistent with that in the war diary, I'm sure we'll hear about that from the Prosecutor in their argument, but there isn't, so you probably won't. Could the crimes in Ahmici be observed in the Hotel Vitez? There's no suggestion in the judgement that they could, and indeed, the evidence in the case is, from Colonel Stuart you could not observe what was going on from Vitez, and from witnesses last week, you heard that even from the inside of a United Nations Warrior, an armed vehicle, looking out through the little round porthole windows, you couldn't see what was going on, you couldn't see that there was a massacre, that there were a large number of civilian casualties, and so forth. And that is contrary to what the Court found below at paragraph 479 of the judgement. Now, it's worth briefly noting that the Trial Chamber also discounted the testimony of the accused when he said he didn't know there was a crime being committed on the morning of the 16th because the Trial Chamber found there was no BH army presence in Ahmici, and therefore, his belief that there was a conflict, fighting, a military conflict, was unreasonable, and they rejected it. The Prosecutor fought long and hard at trial to attempt to prove that there were no BH soldiers in Ahmici, and the Trial Chamber so concluded in the judgement at paragraph 407. You now know from the new evidence, including Witness BA5, that there was a Territorial Defence unit in Ahmici. It numbered 30 to 35 men and it had a significant number of rifles, although not every man had a rifle, most of them did and you heard that testimony last week. And indeed in respect to whether there was fighting in Ahmici, I simply refer you to the testimony last week of two other witness, and I won't go into private session, BA2 and BA3. So that's failure to prevent. What about failure to punish?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Before I go to failure to punish, I should point out that there were no reports to Colonel Blaskic that crimes were being committed on the 16th in Ahmici. And indeed, we know what the reports are. I showed you one written report from Pasko Ljubicic on the afternoon of the 16th. We also have reports of oral communications with Pasko Ljubicic in the war diary, the first -- this is Exhibit 14 to the first -- second, excuse me, Rule 115 motion. The first contact was at 11.42 a.m. on the 16th. It was a telephonic contact from Pasko Ljubicic and he basically said we're in a firefight. No information about any crimes, no information about the destruction of civilian dwellings, no information about the civilian deaths. So false reports were received on the 16th, both oral and written, from the military police with respect to what was happening in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The testimony at trial was that the massacre occurred between 5.30 in the morning and 8.00. So it was over by around 8.00. Now failure to punish. The Defence submits that based on the newly available SIS report, you now know that there was an investigation. The perpetrators were identified. That report went to the political hierarchy, to political and Ministry of Defence officials in Mostar and above, and we submit that that should extinguish or cut off liability of the accused for failure to punish. It would be wrong to convict him for failure to punish when he caused an investigation to be done, he caused the perpetrators to be identified, but that information went to the political and military defence hierarchy, but not to him.
