He didn't get those reports. So he didn't have the information that they had. And furthermore, an alternative basis for you to find that the appellant should be acquitted of any failure to punish liability is that the appellant did not have the ability to punish the military police, under the relevant rules and regulations. While the military police were attached to appellant on the 15th of April, in the case of an all-out attack, the authority to punish the military police remained with the military police administration in Mostar. And for the extensive material and evidence and the appropriate time periods covered by the different military police rules, you can see in our brief, footnotes 95, 108, and 109. And furthermore, the new evidence, which you heard last week, confirms this. Witness Watkins testified that when a unit is attached, in typical military structures, the authority to discipline does not convey with the attachment. It remains with the parent organisation. And I also direct you to the testimony in that regard of Witness BA1. There's also one other documentary piece of new evidence that bears on this, and it is Exhibit 43 to the fourth Rule 115 motion. This is a report to, I believe, the military police administration by the commander of the -- it's a report maybe to various persons. I don't have the face page in front of me, so I don't want to misstate it. But it's a report from Pasko Ljubicic, the commander of the 4th Battalion, and it identifies two individuals who were put into custody, and notes that the conduct of the investigation is under the jurisdiction of SIS, because they are members of the military police. And I'm informed that this is a response to a request from Colonel Blaskic, wanting to know: Are these matters being investigated and the culprits prosecuted? These are -- I can't read the print, but there was -- whether it was displacing Muslims from their homes or property crimes, I don't know which. So here the HVO did not have the authority to discipline and to do what is happening here, but SIS, which is an overarching element of the HVO structure, with a separate command authority, if you will, in Mostar, they had the ability to investigate and to put forward charges against members of the military police. Did appellant take meaningful steps to try to prevent further crimes by the military police after Ahmici? Well, very significantly, the record below is replete with appellant's requests that Pasko Ljubicic be removed as the commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police, and by August of 1993, Ljubicic was removed, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In addition, with respect to Ahmici itself, Blaskic did what he could do identify the perpetrators. Typically, the military police investigate military units that engage in wrongdoing, but here, because the military police was the unit involved, they couldn't do it. The regular HVO had no investigative skills. So SIS was the appropriate authority. And the appellant commissioned SIS with conducting an investigation, and their jurisdiction to do so is set forth in some detail in footnote 137 of our appellate brief. What did he do to cause a SIS investigation? And I note, while we're looking at this time line, that at the time this -- he set this investigation in motion, Colonel Blaskic did not know that the SIS assistant in Central Bosnia, Anto Sliskovic, was involved in the crime. I showed you earlier Sliskovic's report from May 15th, and you compared it with other information, and it obviously was a cover story. But Blaskic didn't know at this time that Sliskovic was in fact a co-conspirator with respect to the crime. This sets forth part of the relevant chronology of the efforts of the appellant to have the Ahmici crime investigated. The crime is on the 16th. On the 22nd, he learns of the massacre. On the 23rd, he wrote a communication that's in the record to Colonel Stuart, proposing some kind of joint investigation. But can the international community and the BH army and the HVO join together to get access to resources of all those entities to investigate the crime? That did not go forward. The international community was very suspicious of the HVO at this time, as one can appreciate. So the next day, the 24th, Colonel Blaskic gave a verbal order to SIS to investigate. On the 27th, as you heard, he toured part of Ahmici with an armed escort and then spoke out and denounced the crime at a press conference that was televised. And then on the 30th, he briefed General Petkovic, his commander, in person, on the Ahmici crimes and gave a second verbal order to SIS to investigate. So those are the events in April. Then in May, the testimony at trial was that from the 5th to the 9th of May, Colonel Blaskic continued to press SIS for the results to date of the investigation, and when frustrated that he wasn't getting information back from the SIS assistant, on the 10th of May he issued a written order to the SIS assistant, and that is Exhibit D341, which you now see before you, dated 10th of May, 1705 hours, order: Gather all the information and submit a report on the events that actually took place in the village of Ahmici, designating the SIS assistant as responsible for this task. The deadline is 25 May 1993. So that order was issued on the 10th of May, and as the deadline approached, on the 21st, 22nd, and again on the 24th, Colonel Blaskic continued to press SIS. And then on the 25th, he received the document that you've already seen, and that is under seal, D608. And I won't comment on that document, because it's under seal. I already have. Then on the 28th of May, he directed a further investigation, and on the 29th of May, further briefed Petkovic and asked for the removal of Pasko Ljubicic and the reorganisation of the 4th Battalion of the military police, in order to, among other things, remove criminal elements from that formation. Then, from the August to 1994 time period, we see that finally, despite requests by appellant much earlier, on the 4th of August, Pasko Ljubicic is replaced, and then appellant, sensing an opportunity to get a more complete investigation, having removed -- having seen the removal of Ljubicic, on the 17th of August, another written order was issued by appellant, and that is Exhibit D343. This order, also to SIS, directs a further investigation and sets a deadline of the 17th of September, 1993, in paragraph 3: "When a complete report must be sent to me in order to proceed with further procedure in front of the bodies that are in charge." That's a reference to he wants a report to submit to the military prosecutor's office so that charges can be brought against the responsible individuals. Mr. Sliskovic, apparently, was still not very eager to conduct this further investigation as you can imagine, and on the 7th of September, he got a short extension to the 30th, for his report, but on the 30th, predictably, no report is produced to Colonel Blaskic, and instead, the appellant is informed by Sliskovic that the report was done, but it was forwarded directly to SIS in Mostar, and the investigation was no longer Blaskic's concern. We also know that on the 25th of April, SIS officials from Mostar visited Central Bosnia for purposes of conducting an Ahmici investigation. That was testimony from an EC monitor at transcript 10168. And then further, we know that on the 26th of November, you have seen the investigative report of SIS, which was not sent to the appellant but was written by SIS in Mostar, and then even later is forwarded to HIS in Mostar, the 15th of March, 1994. So given all these facts, these efforts, does the evidence support the conviction of appellant for failing to make reasonable efforts to cause an investigation into Ahmici and the prosecution of the perpetrators? We submit no. No reasonable tribunal of fact could so find, even if that is the standard. Blaskic did direct an investigation. He did cause the investigation. He diligently pursued it. That investigation uncovered the participants, including the commanders, Pasko Ljubicic and Vlado Cosic. With that information, the military police administration and the Ministry of Defence in Mostar, they were in a perfect position to commence prosecutions of these individuals. And it should have happened. It should have happened in November of 1993, if not before. The fact that it didn't is not the appellant's fault. He didn't even have the reports that named these individuals. And yet he was convicted for failing to pursue an investigation of the perpetrators. He is not criminally responsible for the cover-up that was perpetrated by the local SIS authorities in Central Bosnia, and then ultimately by political authorities in Mostar and elsewhere. Indeed, I haven't scoured the public record, but I don't know of any other Bosnian Croat official that condemned the Ahmici massacre in the way that Colonel Blaskic did at the press conference, according to Martin Bell, on the 27th of April, 1993. I didn't -- I haven't seen that in any press releases or statements from any Bosnian Croat officials in Central Bosnia, in Mostar, or elsewhere in Herzegovina. He's the only one that spoke out and said this was wrong, it was organised, and the culprits must be pursued and punished. And yet he's the one, he's the one who was convicted for failing to try and bring about an effective investigation and prosecution of the culprits. That concludes my comments on Ahmici, and if there's no inquiries from the Court, I will move on to other parts of the Vitez municipality. First, Stari Vitez. The Trial Chamber concluded that there were crimes in Stari Vitez on the 16th of April, that some houses were looted and torched, and that several cafes near the yellow building were looted and torched, burned. That's in paragraph 499. There were no criminal orders by the appellant to commit crimes in Vitez on the 16th. The Trial Chamber reasoned that because appellant gave an order for military action on the 16th, and because crimes were committed during that action, he was responsible. They also dismissed our arguments that the appellant's orders were defensive and legal, and the Trial Chamber found that there were no reports, and I quote, "of any military victims or the presence of soldiers from the BH army in Stari Vitez." That's paragraph 509. And they found in the same paragraph that the Muslim military in Stari Vitez did not put up any defence on the 16th of April. We continue to maintain, as we have for many years, that the appellant ordered lawful defensive military action --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hayman. I understand the interpreters may be have some difficulty in following you. You are going perhaps too quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: My apologies. The appellant continues to maintain that he gave defensive orders on the 16th. They were legal. He never ordered any crimes against civilians in Stari Vitez and that his orders are in the record, D267 and D269. If you find he did not order an attack on Stari Vitez, then there could be no basis for liability for any crimes that followed, based on an order for an attack. If he did order, if you find that he did at some point order an attack on military targets in Stari Vitez, but he did not target civilians, and the attack was proportionate, then there also could be no criminal liability, so long as there was a genuine military target in Stari Vitez. Was there? Well, first, you have the orders, and I won't belabour the fact that there were no orders to attack Stari Vitez, much less to attack civilians. But let's go back to: Was Stari Vitez a legitimate military target? And was the HVO military activity on that day, the 16th of April, proportionate to that objective? This is paragraph 509 from the judgement, where the Court found there were no military installations in Stari Vitez and there were no reports or any military victims or the presence of soldiers from the army. That finding is clearly erroneous in light of the new evidence. Witness BA5 testified last week, and that was an individual in a position to know what military forces on the BH army side were in Stari Vitez, that's where this individual was, that by the 16th of April, the BH army and the Territorial Defence had approximately 220 to 280 soldiers in Stari Vitez. That's at transcript 514. 80 to 100 men of that group were part of a sabotage platoon, transcript 510. They had 220 rifles, four mortars, two machine-guns, one sniper, and ten M-48 rifles, transcript 514. And indeed, the Territorial Defence headquarters was there. This evidence is confirmed by other new evidence. For example, Exhibit 22 to the fourth Rule 115 motion is a BH army report which recounts that in Stari Vitez, defence is being conducted by the anti-sabotage department of Vitez, about 150 soldiers and approximately 50 military policemen. So that's about 200 men, and that's roughly consistent with BA5's estimate of 220 to 280 men. This report is from the 17th of April. In addition, Exhibit 23 to the fourth Rule 115 motion is a BH army report from the 19th of April, in which it states that by this time, a circular defence has been set up in the old part of the town of Vitez and our units successfully beat back the enemy's infantry attacks several times. And that is indeed true. Stari Vitez was successfully defended by the BH forces located there between the 16th and the 19th of April. If there was no defence, then the attacking HVO forces would have just gone in and taken it over. They didn't. The enclave was there for the whole war. And this report confirms that there was -- not only was there a military presence on the part of the BH forces in Stari Vitez, but they were victorious. And then finally, we have Exhibit 4 - excuse me - Exhibit 25 to the fourth Rule 115 motion, a report from 18 April 1993, which indicates that a unit overran the fire station in Vitez and that the enemy had heavy losses. Although I'll have to study that further, Your Honours, to see where that is in relation to the line around Stari Vitez. We'll come back in our argument to you, if that needs to be further clarified. I need to see a map of exactly where the fire station is. When joined with the evidence at trial, we submit the conclusion that Stari Vitez was a legitimate military target is indisputable. The Hotel Vitez was about a hundred metres from the confrontation line. That's well within range of snipers, or these M-48 rifles that you heard about, not to mention mortars and so forth. We understand why the Trial Chamber found that appellant was responsible for this collateral damage in Stari Vitez. The Trial Chamber believed that Blaskic had ordered an attack on Ahmici, and the Trial Chamber believed that there was no BH army presence in Stari Vitez. And it's not a long leap to then conclude that appellant was responsible for civilian casualties in Stari Vitez, but in fact neither of the predicate assumptions were true, and the conclusion is also not true. What about proportionality? Military action is lawful if it has a military objective, and unreasonably disproportionate harm to civilians is avoided. With respect to Stari Vitez, the judgement contains no analysis of proportionality. The new evidence clearly indicates that the military activity in and around Stari Vitez was proportionate. BA5 testified that the BH troops in Stari Vitez were quartered in private residences and they used the houses at the beginning of the conflict to conduct their defence. They had not yet dug trenches, so they used houses. They got in windows and shot out of houses and those houses became military objects used for part of the defence. Further, you also were told by BA5, at the transcript 515 last week, that on the 16th of April, whereas three BH army soldiers were killed, indicating military conflict, no civilians were killed. There were only lightly wounded civilians, approximately 10 to 20. And that also appears at the transcript at 515, lines 19 to 21. If you contrast that with the casualties, for example, on the part of the Vitezovi, you know from Exhibit 88 to the first Rule 115 motion that three Vitezovi were killed, three seriously wounded, and ten lightly wounded, in the conflict in Stari Vitez. So the picture that these documents paint, as well as the witness testimony, is there was a military conflict. There were military casualties on both sides. Even if you find that the military activity caused disproportionate civilians casualties in Stari Vitez on the 16th of April, we submit that no reasonable trier of fact could convict the appellant for those acts. How did the Trial Chamber get there? The Trial Chamber inferred that appellant must have ordered an attack on civilians because the action was well organised and used military tactics, such as an artillery attack followed by infantry. That's at paragraphs 503 and 504 of the judgement. As Mr. Watkins testified last week, the use of mortars, followed by infantry, or artillery followed by infantry, is simply evidence of standard military tactics. There is no causal connection between any order given by the appellant and any crimes that occurred in Stari Vitez. And that concludes my remarks on Stari Vitez with respect to the 16th. I will now go to the 18th, and the tanker bomb. There's been a lot of discussion in the briefs about whether the tanker bomb, was it petrol, was it explosives? We submit to you that's not the real issue. The real issue is who did it and at whose direction? Because quite frankly there was plenty of petrol around and there were plenty of explosives around, as I will indicate from the record in the case. But you have heard, and indeed it was not disputed below, that the Vitezovi carried out the truck bomb. The Prosecutor conceded that at trial, reporter's transcript 24664. Now, you have a wealth of evidence before you, indicating that the Vitezovi basically did what they wanted. If they preferred -- they initiated their own actions at times, and if they didn't want to follow instructions from appellant, they did not. And I'll get to that body of evidence in a bit. But first: The Trial Chamber found that appellant was the only one empowered to authorise the use of the assets and get the quantity of explosives necessary to carry out the truck bombing. Paragraph 530. You heard last week from BA5 that the head of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic, personally selected the driver, the poor individual who was apparently handcuffed to the steering wheel in the tanker and who lost his life in the truck bomb. What else do we have, though? Do we have any more new evidence? We have one piece of trial evidence and one piece of new evidence that bears directly on whether the operative zone command had knowledge in advance that there was going to be a truck bombing. The first of these exhibits is D304, an operative report relating to the day of the truck bomb, indicating that at about half past 1700 hours, there was a terrible explosion and we don't know what it is. They're speculating that it's a grenade, et cetera. That report is confirmed by the war diary, Exhibit 14 to the second Rule 115 motion, when at about the same time, 1720, they actually thought in the operative zone that the headquarters had been hit by an artillery shell because of the violent explosion that they felt. There was an explosion. It was not an artillery shell. It was the truck bomb. So we submit to you there's no basis upon which to infer in any way that Colonel Blaskic ordered this terrorist criminal act. But assume otherwise. We don't think you should, but there's been a lot of discussion about petrol and explosives, so I can't leave it alone at this stage of the case. There's plenty of evidence that the Vitezovi, they had access to not only petrol, they had lots of access to explosives. If you look at Prosecution Exhibit 242, an ECMM report, at page 29, the author of that report noted that in Vitez there is an explosives factory and every tenth man has too much explosives that he has taken. Meaning that explosives were commonly available among the population. And this is confirmed in Exhibit 10 to the first Rule 115 motion, which is a HIS report to President Tudjman, talking about criminal activities and the black market trading of nitroglycerin from the explosives factory in Vitez, as well as Exhibit 31 to the fourth Rule 115 motion, which is a 1 July 1993 SIS report, which specifically links Darko Kraljevic of the Vitezovi to the black market trade in nitroglycerin, et cetera, from the explosives factory in Vitez. So the criminal element in Vitez had access to these explosives, and what the Trial Chamber did was they inferred, well, because this was a big explosion, Colonel Blaskic must have been responsible, because who else had explosives? Well, everybody had explosives, so that logic is not logic that a reasonable tribunal could follow and we urge Your Honours to review that material, because we believe you will reach that conclusion. Now, generally speaking, this is a logical time for me to address whether appellant had effective control over the Vitezovi or whether he did not. Part of the logic of the Trial Chamber below was that it believed appellant had effective control, and therefore he must have ordered the truck bomb. You heard last week, from Witness BA5, that Darko Kraljevic was "frequently out of control." And that it "it would be very difficult" to issue orders and to control Kraljevic. That was at appellate hearing transcript 543 and 544. If we could go into private session for about 20 seconds. I have one additional item of evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, the Prosecutor certainly they've cited in their briefs extensively, and they'll probably show it to you later today or tomorrow, they'll show you the January 1993 order from a higher authority in Mostar, subordinating the Vitezovi to Colonel Blaskic and the operative zone. There is such a document. What I want to call your attention to now is another document, Exhibit 96 to the first Rule 115 motion, in which Colonel Blaskic wrote to the head of the Department of Defence, personally, complaining that this unit, which supposedly has been subordinated to him, has seized a gas station and is selling petrol for their own profit, and he, Colonel Blaskic, is unable to do anything about it. He's powerless. And he's appealing to the Ministry of Defence to intervene because, and using his own words, paragraph 5, "because the Vitezovi commander, Darko Kraljevic, is directly subordinated to you," referencing the head of the Defence department in Mostar. This establishes that even when there was subordination, de jure subordination, there was not de facto effective control. If Blaskic had effective control over the Vitezovi, he would have issued an order to Kraljevic saying: Turn the gas station over to the proper military authorities so that the gasoline can be accounted for, in accordance with military regulations. But instead, he has to beg the Ministry of Defence in Mostar to intervene because Kraljevic obviously is utterly disregarding Blaskic's authority. And indeed, we see again in the reply from the Ministry of Defence, and this is PA26. This is a rebuttal Exhibit from the Prosecutor. It's another order from the assistant chief of the Main Staff, saying again the Vitezovi shall be subordinated. Why did he have to repeat it? He had to repeat it because there wasn't effective control, even though there had already been a subordination order. And I also direct you, in regards to this issue, to the testimony of Witness BA1, at the hearing last week, transcript page 201. I won't go into private session, to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, there are intelligence reports which indicate not only a lack of effective control, but that the Vitezovi commander, Darko Kraljevic, was actively plotting to eliminate Colonel Blaskic and take over his position during relevant periods of time. And this exhibit is Exhibit 4 to the Rule 115 motion, an intelligence report, which documents exactly that, that Darko Kraljevic, who was, we heard from witnesses, he was a drug addict, he was an alcoholic, he was an unstable personality, and he was plotting to get rid of Colonel Blaskic and take over his position. So all of this evidence is inconsistent with the concept that appellant had effective control over the Vitezovi. I also note that with respect to the truck bomb and the Vitezovi, despite the de jure subordination, appellant did not have the authority to punish or discipline the Vitezovi, and thus it's in the record that appellant raised the truck bomb with his military superiors and asked that it be investigated and that the Vitezovi be held accountable for that event. Now I will go, with your leave, to the 18th of July, in Stari Vitez, and I will leave the truck bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You invited kindly the Bench to ask a question at the appropriate time, that the issues stay in context. Is it your intention to address the conclusion found by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 531, last sentence, "At the very least, he took no step to prevent these crimes being committed or to punish the perpetrators." In French, the word these or those crimes do not exist, prevent crimes being committed or punish the perpetrators, in general. He took no step.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Did you say paragraph 571?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The evidence, Your Honours, on that issue is broken down into three components. The 16th of April, the truck bomb on the 18th of April, and the 18 July 1993 attack on Stari Vitez. With respect to the 16th of April, we've gone through the war diary, we've gone through the reports. There were no reports that Colonel Blaskic received on the 16th that crimes were being committed in Vitez. He didn't learn about a crime that he could then act upon to prevent. With respect to the truck bomb, if you look at the war diary, the operative zone command thought they were being shelled. They heard this -- They felt this very great explosion at about 20 minutes after 5.00, and they thought they were actually getting an incoming artillery shell. That event was over in an instant. So when they learned there had been an explosion, the event was over and there was no opportunity to prevent it. With respect to punishment, the testimony from Colonel Blaskic's military superiors, and I believe we showed an exhibit last week to a witness on this, was that Colonel Blaskic raised the truck bomb with his military superiors, indicated he believed the Vitezovi were responsible, and asked that there be an investigation, and indeed the superior confirmed in testimony that there had been an investigation initiated. I note that because the Vitezovi were an attached or subordinated unit, the appellant did not have the authority himself to either discipline them - that follows from the lack of line authority - in no instance did he have the authority to initiate a prosecution, only the military prosecutor could do that. But even as to discipline, the discipline authority it remained with the Ministry of Defence and that is why appellant raised the truck bomb with the Ministry of Defence officials through the Main Staff, his superior, so that an investigation could be conducted. And now I'd like to turn to the 18th of July and address that question in that context. It is appellant's position that he did not order an attack on the 18th of July on Stari Vitez, but at the end of the day, that question is immaterial, because the evidence is very compelling, one, that Stari Vitez was a legitimate military target. So if an attack did occur, the fact of an attack was not illegal. And number two, there were no civilian casualties in Stari Vitez on the 18th of July. And I'll point you to the record in that regard. The Trial Chamber, in paragraph 512, found that the 18th of July attack was illegal because the HVO made use of homemade mortar shells, called "babies," which targeted civilian targets and killed and injured many Muslim civilians. You heard from the testimony last week, from BA5, that, first of all, Stari Vitez had a significant armed formation, 220 to 280 men; that two, after the battle on the 18th of July, there were 26 dead HVO which the BH forces returned to the HVO commanders, and that there were more that lay dead in the field during the summer, attracting the crows; and that in contrast, there were no BH army soldiers who were killed during the attack, and only 15 were wounded. Those facts are provided in the transcript of last week's hearing at 518. Also at 518 to 519, witness BA5 explained that there were no civilians killed during the 18 July attack and indeed only a small number of civilians were lightly injured because by this time they had basements and they had dugouts so the civilian population could seek shelter during military conflicts. Further, with respect to the Trial Chamber's finding that houses were destroyed during this attack and therefore it must have been an illegal attack, Witness BA5 also explained, in the transcript at 545, that by July, Stari Vitez was heavily fortified with a network of trenches and that the trenches actually went in between civilian structures. This was a small area, 500 metres by 600 metres, per Witness BA5. The trenches were in between houses. The BH soldiers were housed in houses. They didn't have barracks. They used houses as their barracks. And in that environment, we submit, if civilian structures are damaged during a military conflict, that is not illegal; that is not improper. If you have houses next to fortifications, if you have BH soldiers housed in homes, then those are not civilian structures per se, and it is not disproportionate if houses in that context are damaged. I also note that there were something on the order of 1.200 civilians living in Stari Vitez at the time, and the fact that no civilians were seriously injured in this attack speaks volumes. So what about the Trial Chamber's conclusion that the use of homemade mortars or bebes was illegal? Well, first of all, the finding that there was loss of civilian life is not correct. BA5 spoke to that. Secondly, was there substantial damage to civilian structures and was that improper? I've talked about where the houses were. But moreover, the use of imprecise weapons, such as a homemade mortar, is not evidence of intent to harm civilians. The fact is, both sides used homemade weapons because at times in the conflict that's all they had. Obviously if you're encircled, resupply is a major problem. We note in the judgement that at 554 and 555, the Trial Chamber recognised that these same homemade mortars were used in the military conflict at Grbavica in September, and yet concluded that that combat operation was lawful. The fact is, most weapons in even the modern army's arsenal are imprecise. There are laser-guided weapons. That's less than 1 per cent of the weaponry that is out there. And to say that imprecise weapons are illegal per se, as the Trial Chamber suggested, would be to say that carpet bombing or other common routine military tactics are illegal. So with respect to failure to prevent and failure to punish liability for the 18th of July, our position is there was no crime on the 18th of July. There was a military defeat by the HVO. They had 26-plus casualties. BH army had some wounded. There were no civilian casualties. There was no disproportionate damage to civilian structures. And with that, I see that I had a section devoted to the very question that Your Honour raised. Let me just review it and make sure that I've covered those points in our colloquy. I'd like to add that in Vitez, as of April 16th, there had not been a prior military conflict in Vitez. There had been conflict in Kiseljak, there had been the criminal activities in January of 1993, but it wasn't a situation where military units in the Vitez area had already engaged in military conflict and had committed crimes such that Colonel Blaskic knew, on 16th April, that units would go out and commit crimes. It was the first military conflict of its type in Vitez. And further, prior to the April conflict - and perhaps this is more responsive to Your Honour's inquiry - prior to the conflict, Colonel Blaskic had set forth a number of orders to HVO military units to try and educate them and put them on notice of what was expected of them in terms of adherence to the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions, and so forth. And these -- some of these orders are set forth in this chart, which identify, at the end, the exhibit number, D346, D347, and D208. And I note that there really is -- I saw in -- well, strike that. Withdrawn. So here are three orders on this slide, and then there are additional orders recounted on a second slide, later in time. 13th February and 17th March, 1993, which is an order to remove any person inclined towards destructive and criminal conduct, take away their weapons and take them out of armed units. So all those orders are before the April conflict, which is relevant, we submit, to the issue of taking reasonable steps to prevent crimes. And I also note that in the war diary, on the morning -- at some point in the morning of the 16th, there's a notation that Kraljevic, of the Vitezovi Brigade, he called in, and appellant specifically directed him: Leave the women and children alone. And I'm not -- I can't recall, as I sit here, any evidence of harm to women and children in Stari Vitez that morning. Hang on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The inquiry is in the war diary, Exhibit 14 to the second Rule 115 motion, at 1741 hours. So at 5.41 in the afternoon, there was this contact, and Colonel Blaskic underscored: "Leave the women and children alone."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I think we have to adjourn now, unless you have a few words to add, but if not, I would prefer to adjourn now and you have more time in the afternoon, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That would be fine. I'm about two-thirds through my remarks, and then Mr. Nobilo, I expect, has about 45 minutes of remarks. So we appear to be on schedule, and I would welcome a break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we'll break now and reconvene at 2.15. May I, before breaking, ask General Blaskic how he feels. Can we continue at 2.15 in the afternoon? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I feel tired, but I believe that we can continue in the afternoon. I am still able to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Blaskic. So we break now and we resume at 2.15. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. So we are now resuming our hearing, and I give the floor again to the Defence, to continue and conclude their submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and we are getting there, I can assure you, in terms of concluding. First, I think the technical difficulties have been resolved and I'd like to try and play the clip of Martin Bell relating what he heard at the press conference on April 27th, so that it can be in the record completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: "Q. Did then Colonel Blaskic address the subject of the massacre in Ahmici at this press conference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes he did. I made some notes at the time which I, with the agreement of the Court, will read. He said he was horrified, he was going to do something about it, that '... a commission is being set up to investigate the atrocities. Whoever did it, did it in an organised, systematic way. It was an organised group of people operating to a plan and therefore controlled by someone. The culprits must be identified and brought to justice,' and Colonel Blaskic said he was appalled." The reference to a commission there is a reference to the written request that the appellant wrote to BritBat, UNPROFOR, on either the 23rd or 24th of April, suggesting that an international -- that a joint commission, including the UN, be established to investigate. So this is three days, about, later. It did not come to pass, but I wanted to explain that reference. Now, returning very briefly to conclude failure to punish, that allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Weinberg would like to have the floor now. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Mr. Hayman, just to this press conference of Mr. -- of Colonel Blaskic: Is there only this witness statement as to the recollection of the press conference, or is there any other evidence as to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were never able to get a videotape of the press conference, Your Honour. We tried. So the best we could do was Mr. Bell's testimony. But I note - perhaps you can see it in the video - he's reading from notes. He had a notebook of notes that he took during the war, and so he was able to read passages straight from his notes, and I believe he said they were, if not verbatim, it was very close to verbatim. JUDGE WEINBERG DE ROCA: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So in Vitez municipality, I said earlier that the record below is that the appellant did inform his military supervisors, his higher-ups of the truck bomb, complained, and asked for an investigation. That is found at transcript 24121 to 24122. And then further, I noted that there was a structure for the investigation and punishment of serious offences by the military, which was in the province of the district military courts, and that legal framework is set forth at pages 88 and 89 of our appellant's brief. Now I will turn to the three remaining Vitez municipality locations that are in the judgement, Donja Veceriska, Gacice, and Grbavica. In each village, the Trial Chamber, as set forth in paragraph 562, found appellant criminally liable "on the basis of his negligence." We do not believe that the use of a negligence standard is an appropriate basis for criminal liability under 7(1). In Donja Veceriska and Gacice, the Trial Chamber found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, my colleague is drawing my attention to the fact, not that you know before pleading, are you aware that the French original text uses the words "dol eventuel"? Dolus eventualis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I recall that at the time. I do not remember the colloquy that we had during the trial about that French term, but we can look at it overnight and perhaps be better prepared tomorrow. Dolus eventualis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you just, for example, compare paragraph 562 in the English and the French version, there you will find in the English version, "negligence," whereas in the French version, "dol eventuel."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Let us take a look at that overnight and try and refresh our recollections, because I recall dialogue about that term during the trial, but we'll have to look back to remember. The Trial Chamber then defined the term, and perhaps this will help today, pending a further review of the French, that the appellant ordered acts for which he could only reasonably have anticipated would lead to a crime, 544, 561, and 562. What actually occurred in these locations? In Gacice, the evidence was that the Vitezovi went into that village. In Donja Veceriska, it was -- I believe there were other units there. And the essence of the appellant's position is there were no orders to do anything inappropriate in these villages. There were, as I believe the Trial Chamber found, there were BH armed units in both villages. They were legitimate military targets. That's in paragraph 543. So there were legitimate military conflicts in both of these villages. And then in connection with that, other things happened that the Trial Chamber found were inappropriate, such as houses were burned, and that sort of thing. But there was no causal nexus between those events and anything directed by the appellant. So that's in essence our position. And we'll take another look at dolus eventualis tonight to brush up on our French. Now Grbavica. Grbavica was also a situation -- this is much later, in September. It's the only event in the Vitez municipality after the 18th of July for which the appellant was convicted. The Trial Chamber found the military conflict at Grbavica was a legitimate military conflict. Grbavica was on a hill, over the road that went from Vitez to Nova Bila, and because the BH army controlled this hill, they had direct sniper fire on the road, and the testimony was the HVO had to actually re-route the road back further to the south, to avoid this sniper fire. So there was a military operation, the objective of which was to control this high ground, and there was a village there, so that the road from Vitez to Nova Bila could once again be used. The Trial Chamber found the military operation was appropriate, legitimate, but that after combat operations were over, again based on a negligence theory, and we'll look at the French in that regard, that there were -- there was looting and burning in Grbavica after combat had concluded. And appellant's position was and is that he was involved, he did direct the military activity, the battle. When the battle was over, the military moved to the new front line and security within the territory was turned over to the civilian police. And I recall a video at trial of people walking around an out-of-control situation where people are taking things out of houses and so forth. But the combat was over. The combat was over. So that is the question there, and we do not believe there's any evidence that appellant directed anyone to loot or burn, or even that he had control or responsibility of the town at that point, because the combat was over. The military action was over. The Trial Chamber also stated that appellant used forces in that action that he knew had been involved in the commission of crimes. The Vitezovi did not participate in Grbavica. The military police had already been reorganised by September. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: (redacted). That's at reporter's transcript 16687, 16694 to 97, and 16702 to 08. Now, the Busovaca municipality, briefly, then I'm going to stop, my colleague is going to address Kiseljak, and then if there's any remaining time, I will come back and address other miscellaneous items. Busovaca, there's not a lot to talk about. The appellant was neither charged nor convicted of any criminal activity in the town of Busovaca, which we believe is significant in its own right. That was carved out of their case. You might ask why. We think it's pretty obvious. But there were two remaining small villages for which the Prosecution did put on evidence and the Trial Chamber did convict appellant, the village of Loncari and the hamlet of Ocehnici. And both of these were charged as events that happened at or about the time the conflict in the area broke out in April; Loncari on the 17th and Ocehnici on the 9th of April, both in April. The Trial Chamber found that it had no evidence of illegal orders related to any burning of homes or deaths of civilians in those villages. That's in paragraph 589 of the judgement. But then it goes on in that paragraph to state: "But then clearly, the Trial Chamber does not have all the orders issued by the accused during the events." So the Trial Chamber presumed that appellant was responsible, based on the scale of the attacks, the timing of the attacks, and that the attacks were operational -- the operational similarity of the events to other HVO attacks. First of all, I note that both of these events involved the military police and they were both small hamlets. Ocehnici was a tiny hamlet made up of 33 people, a total population of 33, some five or six houses. And to suggest that these were part of a large-scale activity and therefore it's a pattern from which one can infer a high-level controlling authority, we believe does not hold up, given the new evidence concerning the military police, the prior use of the military police by Kordic and Sliskovic for terrorist and criminal acts. One cannot infer something because it happened and the military police did it that Blaskic, because he had so-called effective control, he ordered it or was responsible for it. That chain, that logical chain, is now broken and proof should be required. There is no proof. There were no orders. These were tiny hamlets, tiny hamlets, where although any loss of life that is inappropriate is a tragedy still, these events were on a very, very small scale, involved literally a few people and a few houses. The specific evidence that we have, some of it is new. We know, for example, with respect to Loncari, in the 14th exhibit to the second Rule 115 motion, that at 2000 hours the Busovaca Brigade is ordered to go defend Kuber. Kuber was a mountain above this entire area to the north of Busovaca and it's considerably above the villages, including Loncari, which are down below. This is significant because the Trial Chamber believed that the Busovaca Brigade was in Loncari and therefore there was -- even if the appellant didn't have effective control of the military police, the Trial Chamber believed he had effective control of the Busovaca Brigade, and this was an important issue. So we know from the war diary that the Busovaca Brigade is sent to Kuber on the 16th, and then later on on the 17th, in the same war diary, at 1829, that is, about 6.30 in the evening, Kuber was lost. The HVO lost their position on Kuber. Thus, the Busovaca Brigade was there during the day on the 17th, and that is inconsistent with the argument that they were in Loncari engaging in misconduct at that time. With respect to failure to punish liability - because, as I said, everything that appellant was convicted of under 7(1), he was also convicted of under 7(3), which I'll talk about later if there's any time left - both Loncari and Ocehnici involved military police and the Jokers. We do not believe the appellant had effective control of those units. We know he did not have the ability to punish the military police, but we do know he was able, through his urgings, to cause the military police administration to remove Pasko Ljubicic, to install a new commander, and to eliminate the criminals from the military police. So despite the obstacles, he did work to try and improve the conduct and the composition of a unit over which he didn't have control and couldn't simply issue orders to remove a commander or reconstitute the unit. With that, I'm going to turn the floor over to Mr. Nobilo to address the Kiseljak municipality. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as my learned colleague Russell Hayman has just said, I'm going to talk about part of the judgement, which refers to the municipality of Kiseljak. The judgement, in the portion in which it treats the events in the Kiseljak municipality, is not very understandable, so it leaves grounds to the appellant to guess what the legal grounds are for the judgement, which found the appellant guilty of the events in Kiseljak. In paragraph 646 of the judgement, it states that General Blaskic ordered or instigated the crime, which means that he would be held responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute of this Tribunal; although the judgement fails to analyse the command responsibility on the grounds of the theory of punishment, but just looks at it in global terms and terms him guilty by virtue of his command responsibility. And we also note that Article 7(1) is a grounds for the judgement and for finding him guilty. The Trial Chamber, in point 63, states that General Blaskic, even if he did not explicitly order the persecution and killing of Muslim civilians, nonetheless did risk having these inhabitants and their property become the primary targets of the sealing off and defensives launched on the 18th of April, 1993. A conclusion of this kind was brought by the Trial Chamber on the basis of three grounds, and those are the following: The first grounds for a conclusion of that kind was the preparatory and the contents of the combat preparation order and combat order. The second grounds for this was the fact that the orders were addressed to Mijo Bozic, commander, who three months prior to that had already issued an illegal order, contrary to the law. And finally, the third grounds is that he used heavy weapons, artillery, to attack the villages. Since those three groups of facts are the grounds and foundation for General Blaskic's guilt and judgement thereof, we are going to concentrate our efforts on that, and we're going to divide -- I'm going to divide what I have to say into three parts, linked to events that took place in April 1993 in Kiseljak. So the first thing we have to take a look at are the combat orders issued by Blaskic himself. They are documents 299 and D300. One is a preparatory combat order and the second is a combat order, per se. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 641 to 648. Both of these were issued on the 17th of March, 1993. However, for us to be able to comprehend --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a mistake. I meant to say the 17th of April, 1993. For them to understand the importance of the combat orders, we must briefly take a look at what the combat situation was overall on that particular day, the 17th of April, 1993. Regardless of what you might conclude, who it was who on the 16th of April in Vitez pulled the trigger first - probably the military police in Ahmici - I put it to you that the new evidence shows that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the next few days - that is to say, the 17th of April, the 18th of April, the 19th of April, and so on - took over the initiative. If we take a look at the new evidence, which is the wartime diary of the operative zone of Central Bosnia - and that is our second request, and it is Exhibit 14; we have tendered that - then we shall be able to see that already on the 17th of April there is fighting around the HVO brigade headquarters in Zenica and that on that day, the fighting from Zenica was being moved to Podbrezje and Cajdras - that means closer to Busovaca itself - and that on the 18th of April, 1993 the deputy commander of the Zenica Brigade, Vinko Barisic, at 1900 hours, signed the capitulation for the entire brigade. Furthermore, in the diary we shall also see that in the coming days the BH army attacked Busovaca, and I should like to point out document D324 and the wartime diary that I've already mentioned. In D324, this document is a report from the Busovaca Brigade, and in it we can see that 2.000 soldiers - that's what it speaks about - of the BH army are attacking Busovaca. Those soldiers were brought in from various municipalities, including Kakanj, Visoko, which is the neighbouring municipality to Kiseljak. And what does Blaskic do then, faced with a combat situation of that kind? He does what any soldier would do: He tried to open up a second front and, in so doing, to tie in the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to that other front in Kiseljak and, in that way, to weaken the pressure exerted by the BH army on the Vitez-Busovaca enclave. Therefore, document D299 is in fact the first document and the first combat order, which he issues on the 17th of April, at 0910 hours. It is one of two orders on which the judgement is based, the guilty judgement is based. And already, in its title, we will be able to see the purpose of that particular preparatory combat order. What is stated is the following: It is the preparatory combat order to tie up part of the Muslim forces. Let me repeat, to tie down the Muslim forces. It is the military rationale for issuing an order of this kind and not the persecution of the civilian population. In point 1, contrary to the judgement of the Trial Chamber, we maintain that no reasonable court of law in point 1 can find hostile language or incitement to violence of any kind. It is in point 1, as is customary in military orders, that the person issuing the order gives an overview of the situation, and so does Blaskic. The information he received that particular day, he writes down in point 1. And in the war diary that I mentioned earlier on, we have a host of similar information coming in from Zenica speaking about the violence of the BH army against the Croats of Cajdras and Podbrezje. In point 1, there are no expressions of hatred towards the Muslim people, towards Muslims. All that is mentioned is the enemy, and nobody else. For you to be able to understand fully that preparatory combat report, it is necessary to take a look at point 2, which describes the tasks and assignments of the unit of the HVO in Kiseljak, which were issued pursuant to that order, and I'm going to quote here. "The tasks for your unit are as follows: To tie down the aggressor forces by doing the following: A, to block the village of Visnjica and other villages from which the enemy could launch an attack; and B, to take control of Gomionica, Svinjarevo, and previously to lend cannon support, the VBR and mortar fire, multiple rocket launchers; attack the main force from the Sikulje and Hadrovci axis to take control of the defence line and to conjoin all forces." Therefore, in this order, which was the basic grounds for a judgement of guilty, we have clear-cut military instructions. Blaskic is asking that the village of Visnjica be sealed, and he also wants other villages to be sealed off, but he limits this sealing and blocking of these villages to those villages from which a military attack is probable; that is to say, only those villages from which his forces could be placed in jeopardy. And he goes on to say "other villages from which possible attacks by the enemy may be launched." Furthermore, point 2(B) calls for taking control of Gomionica and Svinjarevo. Why? Because it was in Gomionica that the headquarters and main force was located at the BH army in Kiseljak. And according to the position from the judgement, point 632, it was in -- there were 70 soldiers in Svinjarevo of the BH army. And the judgement recognises that in the villages of Gomionica, Hercezi, Svinjarevo and Visnjica, there was a BH army presence there during the relevant period of time. But as we're on the subject of Gomionica, let us now take a look at what Blaskic is asking for. He is not seeking an attack directly on the village of Gomionica. What he says is this: He says that an attack with the main force should take the axis of Sikulje and Hadrovci. Your Honours, in due course, in a subsequent document, we'll be able to see on a map the position of both Sikulje and Hadrovci. They are two hills above the village of Gomionica from which one is able to militarily exert control on villages lower down, on the slopes lower down beneath the hills. So what Blaskic is doing is following military logics. He's calling for the hills above the villages to be taken control of, for him to be able to exert control over the villages down below. Now to conclude this point: It is obvious that Busovaca, during those days, was exposed to an all-out attack. It is also obvious that Blaskic, with this order, sought assistance from Kiseljak. Now we come to the key question that has to be asked: How could the HVO of Kiseljak help and assist the HVO in Busovaca? How was that possible? Only by opening up a new front and to have part of the aggressor forces - from Blaskic's point of view, the aggressor - the BH army, has to be moved to Kiseljak. That's the only way that this could be done, the HVO -- that the HVO Kiseljak could help Busovaca, not the persecution of the population. So this preparatory combat order, contrary to the position taken by the Court, has a purely military logic. It is a lawful one, and it is directed towards the realisation of exclusively military goals. The second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You were kind enough to present to us paragraphs 1 to 5 of this document. However, I want to recall that the judgement, in paragraph 646, makes reference to the eighth paragraph of the same document, saying that, on the contrary, the eighth paragraph implied that this task went well beyond it - the accused employed radical words in the order which have connotations of eradication - "all assault operations must be successful, and to that end use units of the military police and civilian police for the mopping up." These were the conclusions by the Trial Chamber. If you could be kind enough also to elaborate on this eighth point, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll be coming to that a little later on. Point 8 was not in document D299, in actual fact, which represents the preparatory combat order issued on the 17th of April at 0910 hours. Point 8, with this expression of cleansing, is contained in document D300, "mopping up," and it was issued on the same day at 1145. And I'm just about to move to that second document and to explain it, taking into consideration the term "mopping up." So as I've already said, on the 17th of April, the situation in Zenica is deteriorating. The brigade is faced with capitulation, which is ultimately what was to happen, and Blaskic on that same day, that is to say, the 18th of April, at 2345 hours, issued an express combat order for an attack on the next day at 5.30 a.m. So that is the second combat order, the executive one, and that is what the Trial Chamber based its decision on. Now, if we look at military theory, preparatory combat reports and combat -- preparatory combat orders and combat orders, executive ones, should be taken as a whole and viewed together. Now, in this second combat order, D300, in point 1, Blaskic once again engages and analyses the combat situation and enemy activity in that regard; that is to say, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica. If we take a look at the war diary, all the information there -- all the information which Blaskic sets out in point 1, we'll find in the war diary as well. However, there is no mention there once again of any hatred. There is no hatred towards the Muslim people expressed there. There are no serious derogatory terms of Muslims and civilians. All that is spoken about there is the behaviour and conduct of the enemy army, and the enemy army, to Blaskic - we know who that was - were an allied army until very recently, and that is set out clearly in point 1. Furthermore, in point 2, Blaskic orders the use of cannon -- the artillery. We're going to talk about the artillery later on, but I should like to draw your attention to the fact that in point 2, Blaskic speaks about the systematic targeting of the artillery. The systematic targeting of artillery is a notion that is opposite to ad hoc shelling, or random shelling. So what is being done is systematic targeting, which means to shoot at a given target, which is quite different from random shelling, where civilians were killed. Now, what is the goal of that particular combat order? This can be seen in point 4 of the combat order, because it is there that Blaskic specifies the target; that is to say, he pinpoints the enemy and defines it as being the Muslim Armed Forces - and the abbreviation is the MOS, the MOS - and the Mujahedin, which means the members of different -- that is to say, foreigners who came to Bosnia-Herzegovina to fight on the side of the BH army. And it was these Mujahedins that he was referring to. Furthermore, in point 9, the Trial Chamber notes that Blaskic is using dramatic utterances and claims that this is also -- this also constitutes a crime. However, we believe that the sentence contained in point 9, where he urges his soldiers to be aware of their historical responsibility, that no reasonable tribunal could conclude that this is instigation to crime. This melodramatic kind of speech is quite usual in such situations. Let me given you an example: That's Exhibit 45 from our fourth motion. This is an order issued by Mario Bradara, the deputy commander of the Vitez Brigade, in which he orders his soldiers to apply the provisions of the international humanitarian law. So this is without a doubt a positive order, and Mario Bradara further says - let me quote - "Be aware of the importance of your task, because the survival of Croatian people is at stake." Correction: It is not the Vitez Brigade but the Kiseljak Brigade. So Mario Bradara was the deputy commander of the Kiseljak Brigade. So when he issues an order based on the international humanitarian law, he again uses these melodramatic utterances, urging his soldiers to be aware of their task because the survival of the Croatian people is at stake, but he still wants them to abide by the provisions of the international humanitarian law. This is just a melodramatic speech. That's not a crime. Now we come to a very important issue. In point 8, it is stated,

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: the two orders, D299 and D300, point to the same conclusion. Furthermore, in our fourth motion for new evidence, the document 44, is an order -- in fact, it's a report by the other side, of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where they state that they mopped up Gola Kosa. Gola Kosa is the summit -- is a summit en route to Ahmici. There are no villages there, no inhabitants. So if they mopped up Gola Kosa, that could only mean that they had eliminated any HVO strongholds, because there are no villages and no civilians there. The third example: The second motion for the admission of new evidence, document 14, is the war diary of the operative zone Central Bosnia. I will be referring to this document quite often. It is perhaps one of the best things in an evidentiary sense that Blaskic did. He ordered his clerk, at the beginning of the war - we have that in his testimony - that his clerk should write down everything that he sees, everything that happened. So we have a blow-by-blow reconstruction of what was happening. And so on the 17th of April, 1993, at 1035, Blaskic is talking -- at 1635, Blaskic is talking about Gomionica, and he says, "You will have big casualties if you launch a mop-up." That's what he's saying to the Kiseljak Brigade of the HVO. Those who want to expel civilians and fight against civilians cannot have big casualties, but those who enter a village and try to eliminate remaining pockets of resistance in the context of the fighting in a built-up area can expect to have big casualties, which is the best proof of the fact that the term "mop-up" refers exactly to the kind of operation that the military expert described for you last week. This is all I have to say about this issue. However, the Trial Chamber took into account only two orders that we consider to be lawful: the orders of the 17th; we analysed them in full here. However, in order to be able to understand the real sense behind these orders and the mens rea of Tihomir Blaskic at that time, we have to analyse not only the overall combat situation but other orders and other important events that happened at the same time as these orders that are at issue here were issued. On the 17th of April, 15 minutes before midnight, Blaskic ordered an attack to be carried out on the 18th of April, and that's not at issue. He did the right thing, in military terms, because his opponent at the time, General Hadzihasanovic, the commander of the 3rd Corps, did the same thing. In new evidence, Document 47, fourth motion, we have an order, a memo, sent to the Kiseljak unit of the BH army on the 17th of April by Hadzihasanovic, in which Hadzihasanovic says, and I quote: "Check and immediately assess the situation in Kiseljak, and on this basis, with your forces from Kiseljak, disarm and take all the areas taken by the HVO." This is an order issued by the commander of the 3rd Corps, to disarm and to take all the areas manned by the other army is -- automatically means war, because no other -- the other army is not just going to pick up their things and go. Furthermore, Hadzihasanovic says through the authorities that every village should prepare for its defence in its own way, even if it means that they should have their picks and axes ready. In point 8 -- in point 6, it is stated: We expect your proposals urgently, if possible, in the course of the night. Point 7 indicates: Begin preparations immediately. This means that Blaskic made a good assessment when he ordered an attack to be launched in the morning, because that's precisely the same thing that his opponent did, the same order to his own units, for the same day, the 18th of April. In order to be able to understand the orders that the Trial Chamber used as the grounds for the conviction, we have to look at other orders issued by Blaskic in this same period. On the very same day when the hostilities broke out in the municipality of Vitez, Blaskic issued an order, that is on the 18th of April, 1993 - that's D32 - in which he requests all the soldiers to be exchanged for other soldiers and that the information be gathered about those who killed civilians, burned people, and houses. Blaskic is probably inspired by the events in Vitez. But he's not issuing this order to the units in Vitez, but to all the brigades, including the Kiseljak Brigade. Trying to prevent the course of events. So his lawful combat orders, ordering attack operations, must be viewed together with this humanitarian order that he issued on the same day. I will finally go back, and I think that this is really important, to the war diary. And here we have to make an additional effort. Yesterday, when we compared the original handwritten text in the war diary and the official translation into English, we noted that a portion has been left out in the translation. A portion of the conversation between Blaskic and Kiseljak on the 19th of April, 1993. The time was 1635. It is not contained in the English translation, but it is contained in the Croatian text, and I ask the registrar to place the Croatian text on the ELMO. And I would now like to ask -- we don't have the image. We should have the -- so this is the text that is missing in the English version. I will try -- okay. So we have 1635. The entire text is missing. It is very important. I will try to read it, although it is -- it is handwritten. And I would now like to ask the interpreters to try to decipher from the screen, if possible. So the text begins as follows: Kiseljak, Mario calls Colonel TB, obviously this is Tihomir Blaskic - "The area up there has not been taken care of. A little bit remains. Force that. Don't touch the area down there. Visnjica should be sealed off. It cannot be" -- the next word I cannot make out. "Just go along the crest. Do not go down. There is a route. Tell Goran to pay attention to the area up there. We will persevere. We will defend ourselves. Seal off and cut off. You will have large casualties if you do the mop-up. Take the crest. Take from the area down there, from the adjacent units of Goran and from Zoran's facility. This must be the axis. Here things are quite good. Busovaca is being attacked from all sides. You have to hold the forces for them. Provide smaller groups in waves to carry out the tasks."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that, then, was the text of the conversation that Blaskic had over the phone with Kiseljak, and his clerk, at headquarters in the basement of the Vitez Hotel, quite obviously wrote down verbatim what he heard, and this can be seen because you can tell that a live conversation was being recorded, word by word. However, for us to be able to understand this conversation, because the places aren't mentioned, we have to take a look at the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, just to be safe: Is your point that all this item is omitted in the English translation, the whole of what you read out? Because I don't have the text now before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely it, Your Honour. Yes, quite right. In my preparations, I of course used the original Croatian version, and to present it -- the English text to you last night, when we looked through it, we found this missing in the official English translation. So for you to be able to understand this live conversation, we must take a look at the following: The village of Gomionica stretches from the Mlava River valley, rising upwards along the slopes of the hill. Gomionica is at a lower elevation and in a valley as well. Blaskic mentions Sikulje and Hadrovci in his order and we have marked that on the map those are two hills which dominate the area above Gomionica, the hills are up at a high elevation and Gomionica is down below. Now, if we know that, then we can read and analyse the relevant portions, the relevant sentences. And I have extracted for this purpose those relevant sentences. I'm sure you'll remember that Blaskic issued a written order that the units should take control of the two hills, Sikulje and Hadrovci. That is the order what the order read. And from Kiseljak, he's being told that that up there has not been completed, taken care of, which means, in translation, that the hills of Hadrovci and Sikulje have not been taken because that's what it said in the original combat order. Now, Blaskic is responding to a man called Mario from Kiseljak in this case, and he says the following. This is what his answer is: "Force that." Do that. Up there, the hill. That's what he means. And what is most important is what Blaskic says next: "Don't touch anything down below." And that "down below" means the village of Gomionica. Furthermore, Blaskic goes on to state the following: Visnjica has to be sealed off. Visnjica is once again a village that has not to be taken control of, but to be sealed off. And then he goes on to issue the following order: "Take the crest. Don't go down there." Which means go up, up the hill, and not down to the village. And then we come to this very important next point that he makes: "You will suffer heavy casualties if you resort to mop-up. Take control of the crest alone, the slope." And as a reason for all these combat activities, we come to the following sentence: "Busovaca is being attacked from all sides. You must hold their forces. So you must link up the Kiseljak forces, tie up the Bosnia-Herzegovina army forces. You have to tie them down." So this is live speech that we're looking at here. Nothing stylised there, nothing written. This is live, in the throes of battle, speech as it came from Blaskic. So that's what he says at the time, those are the orders he issues to his brigade in Kiseljak. From the new documents, PA47, for instance, PA48, then we have an old Prosecution Exhibit, P456/44, and P456/50, we can come to the same conclusions if we analyse these documents. Those documents lead us in the same direction, just as Blaskic's orders do and what he actually said viva voce. All the more so in document D333, where he says that there was a counter-attack against the HVO launched by the BH army. And furthermore, not only on the 18th of April, but on the 24th of April, orders are issued as they are on the 25th of April, on the basis of the Geneva Conventions. It is number 146/1, 146 of the new evidence and exhibits, D35 is another case in point, et cetera. Now, if we take a look at the report from Kiseljak, D35, then you'll be able to see that there is no information there of any violence against civilians. All we see are combat orders. And let me conclude by saying the following: It is important to note that those orders which provided the basis and grounds for the judgement against Tihomir Blaskic were that these orders were lawful and legitimate, they emerge from military logics in order to accomplish military goals. And amongst the appellant's orders and crime, there is no feedback mechanism, cause and effect. That does not exist anywhere. So no reasonable court of law, on the basis of those orders, would be able to pronounce Tihomir Blaskic guilty. The second grounds upon which the judgement rests is the following, and I'm going to address it very briefly: The fact that Blaskic ordered combat activity to Mijo Bozic, issued a combat order to Mijo Bozic, who, in January 1993, issued an unlawful order. The Court acknowledges that the order never took effect, was never implemented, nothing bad ever happened pursuant to it. But if we were to take a look at the order itself, then what we shall see is this: That it was not sent to Blaskic; he was not even given insight into it, or shown it. And there is absolutely no evidence that Blaskic ever before this trial laid eyes on that particular order. So the existence of that particular order is irrelevant for Blaskic's mens rea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third grounds upon which the judgement finding Blaskic guilty is based is the way in which the artillery was deployed and used, because the artillery was first used and then the infantry. My colleague, Mr. Russell Hayman, has already spoken about that at length. I don't want to repeat what he said. But what I want to say is this: At the trial, nobody presented evidence or showed exaggerated shelling. Nobody showed evidence that there was shelling of civilians. And as I've already said, Blaskic ordered systematic targeting of enemy targets, and not random and non-selective shelling of settlements. Everything that I have said thus far covers the events that took place in April 1993. The next group of events for which Blaskic was found guilty were events that took place in June 1993, in Kiseljak. The Court acknowledges that they do not have a single order by Blaskic for attacks in June 1993, but the Court goes on to say: Yes, we do not have all the documents, and that is correct. They do not. This Court, this Trial Chamber does have the entirety of the documents. The Prosecution can freely go to the archives in Zagreb, look up the months in question, and people spent months there looking through all the documents. There is no order for June 1993. However, we don't accept the position taken by the Trial Chamber and expressed in its judgement that this lack of evidence can go to the detriment of the accused. It is contrary to the fact that everybody is presumed innocent until proved guilty. The guilt of General Blaskic is deduced by the Trial Chamber from the similarity between military operations in April and in June, and especially from the fact that the artillery was used first, that the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade was deployed and used, that the artillery of the Bosnian Serbs was used, and so on and so forth. So this was considered by the Trial Chamber as being similar. We have heard from military experts and other witnesses with military knowledge that this is a basic military technology which is taught in the first year of any military academy in the world. The artillery always goes first and the infantry follows suit. There was no other brigade in Kiseljak except the Ban Josip Jelacic one, and all operations were undertaken by the Ban Jelacic Brigade, the deployment of the artillery of the Bosnian Serbs was Ivica Rajic specialty, and many exhibits testify to that, not those by Tihomir Blaskic. However, what is more important is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would we be able to zoom this map a little more in so we could better follow your arguments? Because it was nearly not legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can see the arrows, and there the hills, denoting the hills, Sikulje, Kocatala, et cetera. On the right we have Sikulje. That was mentioned. A little lower down on the right, at the beginning of the arrow and Kocatala was also mentioned, I believe. Hadrovci aren't on the map, I don't think, aren't shown. However, if you look at the intensity of the lines, map experts can deduce which is the higher elevation, and you can see that the numbers are 759, 770, as features and elevations above sea level, if I can read the map, whereas Gomionica, which is the village, is somewhat lower down. Unfortunately, we weren't able to provide an aerial photograph which would have made things much clearer. Now, if we go on to June 1993 and look at that month, I think we can draw the following conclusion: That Blaskic at that time already had lost de facto control over Kiseljak, the Kiseljak pocket. And one of the key documents is -- as I was saying, we have a new exhibit, number 132, from our first motion, which is in fact a letter written by Blaskic on the 11th of May, 1993, and addressed to -- this is page 2, but I'm -- let me just say that it was a letter sent to Bruno Stojic, who was de facto defence minister of Herceg-Bosna, Milivoj Petkovic as well. That was the second addressee, the head of the Main Staff of the HVO. And Valentin Coric, the police commander. And in it, he says, and I quote: "The situation in Kiseljak is now very complex. That is why I should like to ask you, temporarily, as commander of the Operative Group 2 of Kiseljak, that Mr. Ivica Rajic be appointed to that position, who could, along with your guidance, be in charge of the situation. Because Kiseljak and Kresevo and Fojnica have been cut off from Busovaca, Vitez, and Travnik," and so on and so forth. So what he is doing is proposing that the Main Staff directly lead the operation in Kiseljak via a new function given to the head of Operative Group II to which Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade would be subordinated. And of course if we look at all the other documents we should be able to see that after that particular date, a direct line of communication is being established between Petkovic, head of the Main Staff, and Rajic, in Kiseljak. Rajic informs Petkovic, and then Petkovic issues orders. And that Blaskic was isolated in that communication line. However, de facto, that took place previously, on the 28th of April, 1993, when Petkovic orders Rajic to inform him, report back to him, about the crimes against civilians that had been committed and to inform him, that is to say, Petkovic, the head of the Main Staff. Because Petkovic was in UNPROFOR vehicles and was able to reach Kiseljak through Serb territory. In our documents, you have a whole series of documents that prove this communication, and Petkovic stated in the newspapers, or in other words, Rajic said that he and Blaskic were acting independently of each other and that they were reporting directly to the Main Staff. And the Prosecution knows that the crime in Stupni Do, which was formerly in the area of the Central Bosnia operative zone, yet Blaskic was never charged with this crime, only Rajic.
