In the Kordic case, the Prosecution presented a chart with the system of authorities in this area, that's the document number 16 filed from our motion, where Rajic and Blaskic are shown to be independent of each other, directly responsible to the Main Staff. This is what the Prosecution claims is the case in another case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, by my records, we have until 3.40. That's about eight minutes. Would you like to try to complete that or take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I think you can complete. It's correct you have until 3.40.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. First, I want to clarify the war diary. While my colleague was speaking, I pulled out April 19th in the English, and what I found was the passage from 1635 is there, but the first line, which indicates a new entry, both the time and the contact with Mario in Kiseljak aren't recorded. It simply says "illegible." So a run-on from the entry, but the bulk of it is there, as translated by the translators here today. This is on page 140 of the war diary, Exhibit 14 to Rule 115 motion, second. So we would ask, I think it's appropriate, given that the Croatian version is in evidence, that the translation be corrected. I don't think that would be inappropriate. In effect, it's already been corrected by reading it into the record, but it might be helpful to Your Honours if it were actually corrected in the written exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It may be more appropriate that it be sent to the -- I don't have any objection to it being properly translated. It may be more appropriate that it's sent back to the translation unit for an official translation and brought back. But in terms of the content for today, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That's what I mean, Your Honour. The translation unit. We don't want to do it. So in the five or six minutes I have left, in terms of the legal issues, we would ask the Court to look at the 7(1) versus 7(3) issue. It's set forth in our brief at 118 to 121. That is our appellate brief, in principle, and we simply note the Trial Chamber agreed with our objection that the indictment was vague and contradictory between these two theories and said that the Prosecutor should clarify them or they would bear the consequences of failing to do so. Well, here we are today. So we ask that you look at that, and we also would ask on the legal front that you look at the issue specifically of the failure of the Trial Chamber to find or require specific intent to commit persecution and to discriminate against civilians with respect to the persecution count. We don't believe that that analysis was properly done. So I want to say a word about detention centres and trench-digging, if I have time. I will stop when my time runs out. With respect to the detention centres, Kaonik is one that you have heard about and we think it's fairly straightforward. The appellant had neither de jure or de facto control of this Kaonik facility. De jure control, as set forth in the new evidence, was under -- it was under the district military courts but administered by the military police. This is a report, Exhibit 84 to the first Rule 115 motion, a report by the military police administration to the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban, talking about the military police administration of the prisons. They administered the prisoners in terms of de jure. What did that mean in Busovaca the military police answered to Kordic and Sliskovic. So de facto control of Kaonik was Kordic and Sliskovic. And you can review Exhibit BA4's testimony in that regard in detail if you believe it would be helpful. The Dubravica and SDK detention location was a Vitezovi location. Rotilj was in Kiseljak long after Kiseljak was cut off. I think what's perhaps most important about detention is in Vitez, where Blaskic had relatively more influence, he got all the detainees released by the 30th of April. He signed an agreement on -- he signed an agreement on the 18th of April to release -- for a ceasefire and to release all detainees. That's within 48 hours of detainees being taken. Of course, the problem was, when the conflict broke out, detainees were detained on both sides of the confrontation line. It happened, probably many of those detainees were better off, as a witness testified here last week, because they weren't being killed by criminals and rogue groups that were out roving around. Within 48 hours appellant signed to release them. He got them released by April 30th, in contrast to places like Kiseljak, where he didn't have enough influence to get the detainees released. I would also note the fact of the detention is not illegal. What is the issue and what he was convicted for is inhumane and cruel treatment, and there is no evidence that he is responsible for any inhumane or cruel treatment. We have three slides showing that between April and September of 1993, the appellant issued more than ten orders directing the proper treatment of detainees. We have five orders in April, on the first slide; we have five orders in June, on the second slide; and we have two more in June, one in July, and one in September. Now, the Prosecutor is never going to be content with the issuance of orders, but the question is: He issued the orders. He directed proper treatment and so forth. If it didn't happen, if it didn't get uniformly implemented, why is that? Why is that? Was he supposed to take out a sidearm and start shooting people in the head, taking the law and everything into his own hands? That's certainly not what he was taught at military academy. And he was constrained by his own teaching, for better or for worse. Now, the Prosecutor, we know, in some of their papers have suggested that these orders for proper treatment, they were just a sham. Colonel Blaskic didn't mean it. We've submitted to respond to that orders that were repeated by subordinates, and this is D32. This is an internal order by a subordinate -- actually, this isn't -- we have other orders that are internal. This is one of the orders for proper treatment which are secret, confidential orders. They were created for internal purposes only. There's nothing having to do with propaganda here, and so forth and so on. Now, the Prosecutor may show you PA52, which is dated 27 April, and I would note: Within 48 hours, the appellant issued an order to all brigades to identify and release all detainees and cooperate with the ICRC in this process. That's Defence Exhibit 366. If they want to talk about PA52, which has to do with ICRC access, I would urge you to think critically about this exhibit. Was the appellant charged with denying access to detainees? He wasn't. If so, why are orders like this the ones that are being shoved in your face? Why are they not answering the question: Is D296 illegal? Is D -- excuse me. D267. Is D269 illegal? Is 299 illegal? Is D300 illegal? They should talk about that. Those are the real issues in this case. I will address trench-digging in rebuttal, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Hayman. May I ask my colleagues if they have any question at this stage. Judge Guney, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hayman, still with respect to what took place in Vitez, you indicated that the appellant issued orders to initiate -- something [as interpreted]. Now, my question is as follows -- to initiate an investigation. Now, my question is as follows: Did he initiate several investigations in order to prove effective control, effective control on the part of the appellant? And my second question: If that is the case, what conclusions did these investigations show? Did the appellant ask to get answers by conducting those investigations? Were those investigations launched in order to punish the perpetrators of crimes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have two written orders to SIS to investigate the Ahmici crime. The first was on May 10th, demanding a written report by May 25th. The second was on August 17th, demanding a report by, I believe, September 7th or 17th. And I think if you look at those orders, you can see the frustration -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: I am talking about the orders which were given immediately after the press conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: To initiate --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: To investigate Ahmici, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The orders -- well, the first thing that happened was a request for a joint investigation with the United Nations and the BH army, and that did not come to pass. When that became clear to appellant, he ordered the SIS representative to investigate. That was oral. He, in his follow-up contacts - and this is his testimony at trial - he became anxious that he wasn't getting any feedback, so he issued the written report on May 10. That's the first written - excuse me - written order. That's the first written order to SIS to investigate Ahmici. If you compare that to his August order, you'll see by August he's very frustrated. He uses very strong language. He tells SIS: I want a complete report. I want it in writing no later than -- and he specifies a date in September. I think those orders and his other testimony show he wanted the perpetrators identified. And in the August order, he specifies: I want a report so that it can be forwarded to the proper authorities and so that proceedings can be instituted. That's criminal prosecutive [sic] proceedings, Your Honour. That's what he wanted, and it's in his order of August. I think that -- now, part of your question is: Was he able to - I glean - could he establish effective control over the military police by issuing these orders to investigate? I don't think so. The problem was: He could push SIS to investigate, but he could not discipline, he could not bring charges himself, and ultimately, SIS only reported to him with a dotted line. The SIS's direct line was to the SIS administration in Mostar. So ultimately, in September, the SIS assistant tells him: I finished my report. I sent it to SIS in Mostar. It's no longer your concern. And he could not order SIS to give the report to him, because ultimately SIS reported to the SIS administration in Mostar. So I think he did his best to investigate, but it is not a situation where he could use these limited investigative powers to gain effective control over the military police. He gained much more control over the military police when he was able to persuade the authorities in Mostar, through General Petkovic, to remove Pasko Ljubicic, to install Marinko Palavra and remove the criminal element from that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had a projection on the screen before the map. It was the document you showed before the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: 365 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was it one of the orders to the Kiseljak Brigade? We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Guney is telling me it is the portion of the war diary that was translated -- that was interpreted, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we're talking about the war diary, we know what this is all about. utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're providing the same interpretation to both, that is to say, what you've just said, and also the question asked by Judge Schomburg. So the two terms are used in the same sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. So I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for its submissions in response. We will start now. I propose to have a break at 5.35, for 20 minutes, and then continue until 7.00. And, of course, the prosecution will conclude tomorrow morning. Mr. Farrell.
