utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, honourable members of the Court, good afternoon. As announced by Mr. Farrell, I will start with presenting the Prosecution's oral response to one of the grounds of appeal raised by the appellant. The response this afternoon -- my response will take about 1 hour and 15 minutes. It is going to be a relatively low-tech presentation, but I have made a table of contents of my submissions because they are pretty lengthy. Since I will need to make some reference to closed-session evidence or transcripts, I propose that I will do that towards the end of my submission, and I hope I can be content with making generic references to additional evidence which was given last week. What I propose to cover in the next one hour is our response to Section 2 of the appellant's brief, where the appellant argues that he did not necessarily exercise effective control over all HVO troops. The Prosecution has addressed this ground of appeal primarily in Section 2(B) of its respondent's brief, which is adopted herewith in toto. In my response today, however, I will also have to make reference to written submissions which the Prosecution has given in other parts of its respondent's brief, and I would refer in particular to parts of our response relating to Article 7, both Article 7(1) and 7(3), and also I'm going to briefly address the appellant's arguments that the indictment was fatally defective. What I will do in my submission is to critically review some of the overly generic statements in my submission which the appellant has made in the light of the findings of the Trial Chamber, the trial evidence, as well as the standards prevailing in the Tribunal. I will illustrate my responses with specific examples taken primarily from the judgement. Mr. Farrell will then proceed with responding to grounds 3 through 5 of the appellant's brief and addressing primarily the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's findings in light of the additional evidence. I will now proceed with the first part of my response this afternoon. Insofar as the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. I've been given this index of what is -- the index of your submission, I guess. Do you want it distributed? Did you give it to the Defence as well? Oh, you have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I had given a copy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Insofar as the Prosecution understands the often-convoluted arguments made by the appellant, I understand that two main propositions are made throughout his appeal. Insofar as the regular HVO troops are concerned, the appellant does not appear to dispute that he was, de jure, in command of these troops. However, he seems to dispute that he was always de facto in control of these troops in the entire region. Insofar as the other HVO troops are concerned -- and I'm using this term generically because with the term "other HVO troops," we could refer to special units, such as the Vitezovi and the Jokeri, but there were also troops like the Milici police, which don't seem to fall in any particular category. Insofar as these other HVO troops are concerned, the appellant seems to claim that whilst these troops may have been de jure assigned to him for a particular period or a specific assignment, he did not always exercise either de jure or de facto effective control over them on the grounds that they were reporting elsewhere in the structure, to other units or other persons, or because they would be reporting to no one. The Prosecution's response to these arguments is threefold. Firstly, it is important to remember that the appellant was convicted on the basis that he ordered crimes, under Article 7(1) of the Statute. And this is the first part of my submission this afternoon. Secondly, in the alternative, the Prosecution submits that the appellant's attempts to challenge the elements of his responsibility under Article 7(3) are legally flawed as well. And the third part of my submission, Your Honours, is that the additional evidence which has been adduced does not show that no reasonable trier of fact could have come to the conclusion, A, that the appellant ordered the crimes he was convicted of; and, B, that he exercised effective control over the HVO troops that executed the actus reus of the crimes he was convicted of. And this is the third part of my submission, where I will go to the trial evidence and I would request closed session for the last part of my submission. As the Prosecution has emphasised in its respondent's brief, insofar as the appellant seeks to show that he did not exercise effective control over all HVO troops, there can be no impact on the verdict. The reason for this is that although the Trial Chamber unambiguously found that the appellant exercised effective control over all HVO troops that committed the crimes he was convicted of, the Trial Chamber found that above and beyond his responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute he also ordered the crimes in question. I would direct Your Honours' attention to the part of the judgement where the Trial Chamber sets out its preliminary legal analysis for cases as the present one, where an accused is charged concurrently under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) of the Statute. This is set out in paragraphs 337 through 339 of the judgement. I will not read these paragraphs, but the Trial Chamber says in essence that in cases where a person has been found to have ordered the crimes, it would be illogical to find the person also guilty under Article 7(3). And when we then go to the disposition, Your Honours, we see that the Trial Chamber has essentially come to the following conclusion: That although the evidence on record meets a conviction both under Article 7(1) and conviction under Article 7(3) the primary mode of liability the Trial Chamber thought expressed best the criminal responsibility of the appellant was Article 7(1), ordering. And this is an important preliminary observation, because although we don't think this was the case in this case - and this is the Prosecution's submission - if a person has been convicted of ordering crimes, it doesn't really matter whether the agent or the person executing the crime was or was not under the accused's effective control. Technically, there is no requirement that the agent executing the actus reus of the crimes is a subordinate of the person giving the order. Whether or not the agent or the persons executing the crimes are subordinates is simply not pertinent for the mode of liability of ordering. I will immediately concede, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber in this case appears to have proceeded on the assumption that a strict superior-subordinate relationship is required for the mode of liability of ordering. However, as the Tribunal jurisprudence indicates, this is technically too high a standard, for it is sufficient that the mode of liability of ordering that the accused occupied a position of authority and that he used or she used that position to convince or instruct another one to commit an offence. I'll quickly cite the judgements where this principle is set out. It can be found in the Kordic Trial Chamber's paragraphs 829 and 939 through 941; it was also confirmed in the Krstic trial judgement at paragraph 601; it was confirmed after that in the Stakic trial judgement at paragraph 445; and also in the trial judgement against Naletilic and Martinovic at paragraph 61; and more recently in the Galic trial judgement rendered on the 5th of December 2003. These considerations notwithstanding, even if - and the Prosecution assumes for the sake of argument - the Blaskic Trial Chamber would have heard in finding that the appellant had effective control over certain HVO troops, which is not the case, the appellant's conviction for ordering should not be vacated. Insofar as the evidence shows that he occupied a position of authority and used that position to convince another one to commit an offence. It is our submission that the passages where the Trial Chamber uses the terms "effective control," "command and control," and "superior responsibility" must be read in that light. Technically, it is too high a standard. Your Honours, a careful analysis of the Trial Chamber's findings show that it is precisely the line of reasoning followed by the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber focussed on the accused's orders. It braced particular importance to the orders issued by the accused because these showed, in the Trial Chamber's opinion, whether or not he had ordered crimes or must have considered to have ordered them, what units he gave these orders to. I would draw Your Honours' attention to paragraphs 429 through 432 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber, if you like, sets the tone for its analysis of the appellant's responsibility for the crimes in Ahmici. The Trial Chamber starts with examining the accused's orders. In paragraph 433, the Trial Chamber looks at order D267, which was on the face of it addressed to the military police, the Vitezovi and the HVO operative zone brigades. And this was also confirmed at trial by Defence witness Slavko Marin, who was the appellant's own chief of operations, a direct subordinate. The second order the Trial Chamber looked at is analysed in paragraph 434. It's order D268. The Trial Chamber correctly pointed out that this order was addressed to the Viteska Brigade of the HVO and to the military police 4th Battalion. The Trial Chamber noted that these units were asked to ensure that combat readiness be increased to the highest level and that they were to take defensive action. I will not read this paragraph in its entirety, but I would only like to draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to the last phrase of this paragraph: "The accused admitted that action could be taken by virtue of that order in particular to combat terrorist activities." And you will recall, Your Honours, that last week during the additional evidence hearing Witness BA3 confirmed in response to a request from the Bench - and I believe it was a question put to the witness by Judge Guney - that if a person is authorised to order a unit to take defensive action, that person must also be considered authorised to order that unit to take offensive action. Let me continue with the Trial Chamber's paragraphs. The third order the Trial Chamber focuses on, in paragraph 435, referred again to planned terrorist activities. And it cites the risk that the enemy is engaging in an open offensive to destroy - and I quote - "everything Croatian." It's addressed to the Viteska Brigade and to the Tvrtko independent units. It asks those units in the event of open attack activity by the Muslims to neutralise them and prevent their movement with precise fire. That order, as the Trial Chamber correctly noted, indicated that the forces of the Milici police 4th Battalion, the Zrinski unit and the civilian police would also take note in combat. Footnote 917 to that paragraph shows that the Trial Chamber based its interpretation of terms used in that order. It says something to the effect of: "In front of you are the forces of the 4th Milici Police Battalion, to the right of you are these and these forces. You will recall, Your Honours, that last week, Witness BA1 confirmed that this language is similar to language that would be used in a western army in order to prevent from troops engaged in combat from shooting at each other. The fourth order the Trial Chamber looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. May I -- of course, you didn't invite us, but may I ask you one question on the paragraph you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned paragraph 435, and in the last sentence it reads: "The order closed by saying that the instruction given previously should be complied with, although the Trial Chamber was not able to establish what was the instruction."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you elaborate a little bit on this. It seems to be a little bit difficult, based on this, to identify what was the concrete instruction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree, and I don't have an immediate answer to your question, but the purpose of my submission is to show that the language used in these orders was language showing that the appellant issued orders which would, in a normal understanding of the terms, be understood as leading or enabling a unit to take -- to take part in combat operations. That is the purpose of my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: In paragraph 436, the Trial Chamber notes that following the ceasefire agreement, the appellant issued an order to the NS Zrinski Brigade to stop fighting immediately. These four orders alone, Your Honours, show in a nutshell that the appellant issued orders, combat orders, offensive or defensive, to a variety of troops, regardless of his arguments about de jure or de facto subordination of the troops to him. In fact, in our submission, Your Honour, these four orders alone support the Trial Chamber's conclusions in paragraph 752. To achieve the political objectives to which he subscribed, General Blaskic used all military forces on which he could rely, whatever the legal nexus subordinating them to him. And one could be forgiven for getting lost in the names of the units at issue, but I would recommend, Your Honours, to look at the tables which were provided in the beginning of the judgement, which show that two of the brigades just mentioned in the four orders were regular brigades. They are the Viteska Brigade and the Nikola Subic Zrinski Brigade. Two other units that are mentioned in the orders are special units: The Vitezovi and Trvtko. And then, as I said earlier, the military police seems to be in a category apart. I would also refer Your Honours to a part of the Prosecution's closing brief at trial, where the Prosecution has set out in detail a description of these units. And the reason why I'm mentioning this is that it has been mentioned last week, and also today, that there would be nothing special to the offensives starting with an artillery offensive. One of the witnesses was asked last week for his opinion on that, and he said, "Well, that is a normal military operation. Every military operation, any country, starts with an artillery offensive followed by an infantry offensive." Your Honours, the Trial Chamber was correct in attaching special significance to the evidence that the offensives would start with artillery units, because there is little dispute that in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone the artillery units were placed directly under the appellant's command. That is mentioned in our closing brief, and there's also reference to the transcripts which support this. Of course, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber did not only examine as to whether the appellant, A, had issued orders; B, as to which units these orders were directed to. The Trial Chamber also assessed whether, C, these orders had been executed by the units in question; and D, whether the units had gone beyond the accused's orders. Taking again the four orders in question, the Trial Chamber's analysis of point C and D is set out in paragraphs 437 and following of the judgement. I will summarise the elaborate findings made by the Trial Chamber on these questions, and I will return to these paragraphs at the end of my submission. The Trial Chamber concluded that the evidence showed beyond a reasonable doubt that the units the appellant had given orders to had indeed committed the crimes in question; and B, that the crimes were committed pursuant to his orders. At the same time, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber went further. It also examined and dismissed the appellant's arguments that he was not in effective control of the regular units he gave orders to, that the HVO was disorganised, that there were insufficient means of communication. The Trial Chamber's findings on this can be found in paragraphs 442 through 448 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber also examined and dismissed the appellant's arguments relating to the special units. He claimed essentially that they were not in his de jure and/or de facto control. The Trial Chamber's findings on this can be found in paragraphs 449 through 456. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber had overwhelming evidence before it to conclude that the appellant should be found guilty under Article 7(1) for having ordered the crimes in Ahmici. However, the Trial Chamber went even further and also made findings for two alternative bases of responsibility. The first one is whether there was enough evidence to find that even if one would accept that he had not ordered the crimes through direct intent, that he was guilty on the basis of indirect intent. That is to say that he ordered an action, knowing and accepting the risk that such crimes may be committed, as he was perfectly aware of the criminal propensity of the troops he had selected for the attack on Ahmici. The Trial Chamber's findings on this can be found in paragraphs 474 through 476 of the judgement. The other alternative basis of responsibility the Trial Chamber examined was his responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Trial Chamber examined whether there was enough evidence to find that even if he cannot be considered to have ordered the crimes through direct or indirect intent, whether there was sufficient evidence on the record to enter a conviction under Article 7(3) of the Statute, on the ground that he knew or had reason to know of the crimes committed and failed to prevent or punish the perpetrators. The Trial Chamber answered both these questions in the affirmative. Its response to the last question can be found in paragraphs 477 through 494. To return, Your Honours, to the preliminary observation which I made in the beginning of my submission: Does it matter whether the Military Police 4th Battalion was or was not in the appellant's chain of command? Your Honours, it would only matter if, contrary to the overwhelming evidence on record, he did not issue orders to them for combat operations. It would only matter if, even if he had issued orders to them, his orders had not been executed. But the overwhelming evidence on record says otherwise. It would only matter if, even if he issued orders to them, and even if the orders were executed on the ground, they were not executed pursuant to his orders. But there is overwhelming evidence on record to say otherwise. Your Honours, I could go through the same analysis for the other municipalities and the other incidents the Trial Chamber analysed. I would just like to refer you to paragraphs 516 through 518 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber summarises its conclusions in relation to the incidents in Vitez and Stari Vitez. The Trial Chamber first analysed the orders given by the accused and then it went over to the analysis for the alternative basis of responsibility I have just discussed. If you'd allow me to say a few words on the indirect standard. The Prosecution -- the indirect intent standard. The Prosecution is in a difficult position, since we haven't heard the appellant's oral submissions on this one, but the appellant has made written submissions on the indirect intent standard used by the Trial Chamber. And I will just restate the Prosecution's response to this, but I would ask for leave to make further submissions on this tomorrow, after we have heard the appellant's submissions on this one. Insofar as we understand the written arguments made by the appellant in the appellant's brief, the appellant, first of all, stated that for ordering, a specific intent requirement is required, its desire to commit a crime. We have responded to that. Ordering does not require a specific intent requirement. The second or alternative submission the appellant seems to make is that the Trial Chamber adopted an erroneous standard of recklessness or negligence or in erroneously watered-down dolus eventualis standard. Your Honours, in the Prosecution's submission, the standard adopted by the Trial Chamber for indirect intent, in case one could not say that the accused intended the crimes to be committed, the Trial Chamber in this case adopted a perfectly adequate indirect intent standard. It is a standard which is adopted by this Tribunal. It doesn't resemble maybe the dolus eventualis standard from one or the other national jurisdiction, but the indirect intent standard which has been applied by this Trial Chamber has been confirmed by a series of judgements. And we would also submit it's the indirect intent standard which has also been confirmed by the Tadic and the Krnojelac appeal judgements. And if you allow me just to refer to the paragraphs of the judgements which confirm this standard. The Tadic Trial Chamber adopted a similar standard in paragraph 688. The Celebici Trial Chamber, in paragraphs 327, 328, 378, and 420 through 439. It's a standard which has been set out by this Trial Chamber at paragraphs 278 and 474. It's also the standard which has been adopted by the Kordic Trial Chamber at paragraphs 229, 236, and 386. It's a standard, Your Honours, which also can be found in the Kvocka trial judgement at paragraph 251; in the Galic trial judgement at paragraph 172. And, in our submission, it is a standard which was given by the Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 220 and which was confirmed by the Krnojelac appeal judgement at paragraphs 32 and 121. The language used by these judgements may differ, but in our submission, the standard is clear: awareness of substantial likelihood that the criminal act or omission may occur, and willing or conscious acceptance of that risk. Your Honours, insofar as we understand the appellant's written submissions, the appellant seems to say that the standard for indirect intent that should be adopted by this Appeals Chamber is the one which followed from a series of cases from one particular national jurisdiction. And I will not elaborate too much on that one today. Our submission is that the standard which comes from that jurisdiction is in theory higher, but in practice, when supplied [sic] to the similar cases as we have before us today, the standard is closer to a recklessness standard, at least a standard that has been adopted by this Trial Chamber. The appellant seems to like, in particular, the case-law where lower-ranking soldiers have been acquitted of attempted manslaughter, in cases where there was evidence that they took evasive action so as to prevent death from occurring. This is, of course, not the situation which is before us here today, and there is no requirement in our jurisprudence that the Trial Chamber makes a finding that the accused hope that a certain result would not occur. And, Your Honours, it is beyond comprehension how a general who orders attacks of a village could justifiably hope that serious violations of international law, such as murders and cruel and inhumane treatment, would not occur. Your Honours, if the appellant makes further submissions on the indirect intent standard adopted by this Trial Chamber, I would seek leave to make a further response on this issue tomorrow. I will quickly make a submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Ms. Boelaert-Suominen, you want to make further responses, but I mean you yourself are responding to the written submission of the other party. How can you claim to have a right of further response? I mean, it's not in the proceedings we normally follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If you want to elaborate, you can elaborate as far as you want now. But -- and then the appellant will have a chance to reply, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. With your permission, I would like now to deal with the last point mentioned in my table of contents; it's the question whether or not orders need to be unlawful on their face. During last week's additional evidence hearing and also today the appellant has mentioned that he could not be found guilty as the orders were not unlawful on their face. And as far as we understand the appellant's submissions in this regard, he seems to rely on the jurisprudence coming from the high command case. Your Honours, we have responded to this in our respondent's brief. The high command case is not applicable to the appellant's situation. The requirement that orders need to be unlawful on their face is a requirement which serves to protect the interest of subordinates in the chain of command who are given an order to execute. It is not meant to protect the person who issues the order. The appellant, Your Honour, is not General Wilhelm von Leeb. There is no evidence on the record that he would have protested against the unlawfulness of an order. Your Honours, I will now start with the second part of my submission, and it deals with the arguments relating to Article 7(3). Your Honours, the questions which may arise after my submissions on the first part is whether there is a need to address Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Prosecution's submission is that there is a need to do so. As stated earlier, the Trial Chamber in this case used the standard of effective control in relation to the mode of liability of ordering, although this was technically, legally too high a standard. It is a lens through which the Trial Chamber assessed whether the appellant had the authority and used that authority to issue orders. The second reason is that the Trial Chamber, as I mentioned earlier, when you look at the disposition, concluded that on the basis of the evidence before it he could also be convicted under Article 7(3) of the Statute. And the Prosecution wishes to make an alternative submission in this regard. To the extent that this Chamber may be of the view that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he ordered the crimes, it is the Prosecution's submission that your competent to revise a conviction and find the appellant guilty under Article 7(3) of the Statute for all counts. There is no problem with notice here, as we have demonstrated in our respondent's brief. The appellant made an argument that this should lead to an acquittal on all grounds -- on all counts, on the ground that the Trial Chamber would have adopted an erroneous legal standard for the had-reason-to-know aspect. The Prosecution has addressed this in its respondent's brief as well. This case, the trial -- the Blaskic case was run on the basis that under the had-reason-to-know standard for military commanders, a commander could also be found guilty under what is known as a should-have-known theory, where in case a commander did not have the information in his possession, he could be faulted for not having collected this information in the first place. The Blaskic Trial Chamber concluded in theory that the should-have-known theory, which is basically a negligence standard, formed part of the mens rea under Article 7(3). The Celebici Trial Chamber came to another conclusion. This issue came then before the Celebici appeals judgement, and the Celebici Appeals Chamber has decided that the should-have-known theory is not one of the hypotheses a Trial Chamber in this Tribunal can take into account. We have recognised this in our respondent's brief. However, Your Honours, there is no impact on the verdict. There is not a single finding in the judgement that rests on the should-have-known theory. In all instances where the Trial Chamber goes to the evidence of whether or not the accused knew or had reason to know about the crimes, the findings are based on knowledge, direct or circumstantial evidence. Secondly, Your Honours, I would submit that whereas this Trial Chamber adopted the should-have-known theory, should-have-known hypothesis and theory, some of the criteria which it used are also criteria which the Celebici appeals judgement later said met the had-reason-to-know hypothesis. For instance, in paragraph 328 of the Blaskic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber says that "If there is information about the tactical situation, the level of training and instruction of the subordinate officers and their troops, as well as their character traits, that this could support a should-have-known theory." The same factors were later cited by the Celebici appeals judgement showing a had-reason-to-know inquiry notice standard. But the main submission on this one is, Your Honours, that there is no problem with finding on the evidence that the appellant could be found guilty under Article 7(3) of the Statute. With your leave, I will now address some of the elements of Article 7(3) responsibility. The appellant often seems to claim that he was not the superior of certain troops as they reported to someone else. We've heard reporting lines to Mostar, Grude, to Kordic. The Prosecution response to these type of arguments is as follows: The fact that certain HVO troops or certain units may have had other masters apart from the appellant himself does not show that the appellant must be exonerated. Our jurisprudence sets out very clearly that in cases where the subordinate perpetrator was under the command of more than one superior, both of them may be held responsible for the same crimes. And I will just refer to one judgement only, because there's a series of judgements which states this. You have the Aleksovski judgement, for instance, at paragraph 106. In this connection, you will recall, Your Honours, that last week several witnesses testified that in their opinion Kordic was some sort of political superior, another type of superior to Blaskic. This is entirely consistent with the evidence before the Trial Chamber. In the final analysis, which is a legal analysis, even if the appellant were able to show that certain units reported to Kordic, it does not matter if there's also evidence if the same units also reported to the appellant. Similarly, Your Honours, last week we heard testimony that a superior of the appellant was in a particular region and dealing closely with a subordinate of the appellant. I will not refer to this testimony, but Your Honours there's nothing sinister about a superior of the appellant dealing directly with a subordinate of the appellant if they're in the same region. Your Honours, the question of the appellant's ability to prevent and punish; it's an important question. The appellant's main submission at trial but also on appeal has been that he was not legally competent to investigate and punish crimes committed by certain special purpose or other units. Your Honours, the Tribunal's jurisprudence shows that a superior can be found liable as soon as it is demonstrated that this person was able to take an important step in the disciplinary process; for instance, by submitting a report to competent authorities. The jurisprudence on this is very settled. I would also -- I could cite a number of judgements which confirm this principle, but maybe I can be content with citing one, the Kvocka trial judgement, at paragraph 315. In this connection, Your Honours, you will recall that last week, during the additional evidence hearing, the appellant tried to have witnesses comment on the legal standards adopted by this Tribunal to measure effective control. Witness Watkins, for instance, said in response to a question -- the question was as follows: "Are you saying that mere ability to get reports and issue commands is not enough to have effective control?" His answer was: "It's not enough to have effective command and control." Your Honours, with all due respect, it is not up to a witness to comment on the legal standards adopted by this Tribunal. A superior can be found to have effective control if he can take an effective step in the disciplinary process. One can perhaps have some sympathy for why a military professional would feel uncomfortable with this standard. However, ultimately it is up to a trier of fact, the Trial Chamber in the first place, to determine whether the ability to file a report amounts to an effective step in the disciplinary process. In this connection, I would also like to draw the Appeals Chamber's attention to paragraph 338 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber cites a provision of the Yugoslav armed forces regulations, which in effect adopt a similar standard. And if you permit me to read this, it says, in the English translation: "The commander who knows that the violations of the law of war took place and did not charge those responsible for the violations is personally responsible. In case he is not authorised to charge him and he did not report them to the authorised military commander, he would also be personally responsible." In this case, of course, there's little doubt that this standard was met on the evidence. The most effective course of action open to the appellant, the Prosecution submits, would have been not to use troops accused or suspected of crimes for further military operations. Now, I will turn to this issue later, Your Honours. But for present purposes it may be sufficient to note that the appellant, even when he claimed that he suspected the military police of having committed the crimes in Ahmici used the same troops for the Busovaca operations on the 17th and the 19th of April and also for the operations in Grbavica in September 1993. The same goes for the Vitezovi. Even if the appellant claims that he suspected that the Vitezovi had committed the crimes in Vitez and Stari Vitez, the evidence on record shows that he continued to deploy them throughout the summer. The appellant insists that the evidence on record -- the new evidence on record shows that these units contained criminals. Your Honours, this was not new evidence. This evidence was before the Trial Chamber. The simple question is: If he knew, why did he continue to use them for military operations? He could have filed a report or he could have decided not to redeploy these troops. More importantly, Your Honours, the evidence on record as to the appellant's legal powers to prevent and punish all HVO troops is abundant. We have not heard much about these statutory and regulatory sources of the control of the appellant, but they are set out in detail in the Prosecution's closing brief, Book 2, Part 3, Section 5. We do not have the time to go over all these sources in detail, but I would like to summarise for you what I regard as the most important points of these regulatory and other sources of control, in the light of the appellant's arguments on appeal. First of all, the fact that the appellant had these disciplinary and other powers was supported by evidence on the record. I would especially refer to Prosecution Trial Exhibit P38, tab 2, and the other exhibits mentioned in the Prosecution's closing brief. There was also compelling testimony on this issue coming from what I would call HVO insiders. There was one court witness whose name I cannot mention, but I will return to this person in the closed session part of my submission. There was also a Defence witness, Mato Tadic. He was an official in the Ministry of Justice of Herceg-Bosna, and also, unless I'm mistaken, a deputy prosecutor of the military disciplinary court. And there was also Defence witness Slavko Marin, the appellant's own chief of operations, who confirmed on record the appellant's legal and another authority to prevent and punish. The protected court witness, Your Honours, confirmed that the appellant did have the competence to discipline members of the military police and members of special purpose units. In the text of the rules of the military discipline themselves -- and I'm referring, Your Honours, to Article 52 of Exhibit 38, the Prosecution Exhibit 38 at trial, tab 2, and I'm just going to read the excerpt. It says that: "Rules of military discipline applied either to units which were subordinate to the operative zone commander or units which are within the area under the operative zone commander's authority." This was a simple text, and the meaning of this text was confirmed by the witnesses who testified on this issue at trial. The regulations, which are discussed in our closing brief, obligated the appellant to preserve and collect evidence in case of evidence of crimes. He was also required to arrest persons whom he suspected had committed war crimes. And on top of that, Your Honours, he also had de facto powers of a disciplinary nature which exceeded the legal powers but which he continually exercised. There is evidence on record that persons were complaining about the appellant exercising disciplinary powers which he did not possess according to the regulations. Your Honours, the appellant also had the competency to appoint and dismiss subordinates, and this was a power which he exercised frequently. You will also find in our closing brief a discussion of this, an example of this, when the appellant dismissed Stjepan Tuka, because as far as the evidence shows, this commander refused to introduce war into the Kiseljak region. The appellant did not hesitate to dismiss this commander. Your Honours, it is not a necessary prerequisite for superior responsibility that the commander had the sole power to take all necessary steps to prevent -- necessary steps to punish the relevant subordinates. In this connection, Your Honour, you will recall that last week witnesses were asked about what the lack of communications meant for effective control and whether command always brings control. Witness Watkins responded to this question. For effective military operations, there are three Cs, as were thought in the Western armies, that is, communications, command, and control. Witness BA1 responded: Command does not always bring control. Your Honours, my learned opponents' attempts to elevate military jargon to legal standards were dismissed by the Trial Chamber, and they should also be dismissed, in our submission, by the Appeals Chamber. In any event, the Trial Chamber in this case thought that the three Cs were in place in the days following, and even prior to, the 15th of April, when the appellant's troops attacked 20 villages in the space of less than five days. The Trial Chamber's findings on this issue are set out in paragraphs 386 through 393 of the judgement. I will not go into this. Similar findings can be found in relation to Vitez and Stari Vitez. And you will recall, Your Honours, that last week one of the witnesses confirmed that for an operation of this scale, in his opinion - and he was a professional - 15 to 20 days' prior planning was required. And the Prosecution would also recall that there was ample evidence before the Trial Chamber showing that the appellant had the communications necessary, despite temporary physical separation. And I refer to the evidence put before the Trial Chamber in Book 2 of the OTP's closing brief, Part 3, Section 2, IV. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber in this case did what the Tribunal of Judges needs to do: assess whether the evidence meets the legal standards prevailing in this Tribunal in order to find a person guilty under Article 7(1) and 7(3). It duly considered the arguments put forward by the Defence and rejected them for the reasons set out in the judgement. The Trial Chamber looked at the evidence and dismissed the relevance of this military terminology not because they would not be significant in military terms but because in legal terms, in view of the standards this Tribunal need apply, they were relevant. I would refer Your Honours to paragraph 520 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber dismisses the distinctions which the appellant sought to make between the notion of temporary subordination and that of permanent attachment in relation to the Vitezovi. The Trial Chamber simply noted that he had the ability to give them orders and that he had the ability to receive reports and to report on them regarding potentially criminal activities. The Trial Chamber's legal analysis, in relation to the appellant's link, for instance, with the Vitezovi units, I submit, is correct from a humanitarian's perspective as well. This is what the commentary of the ICRC on Article 87, paragraph 1 of Additional Protocol I has to say about the responsibility of a commander over troops which are not normally under his command. The commentary says - I'm just quoting an excerpt - "A commander may for a particular operation and for a limited period of time be supplied with reinforcements consisting of troops who are not normally under his command. He must ensure that these members of the armed forces comply with the conventions and the protocol as long as they remain under his command." And this commentary was endorsed by the Celebici appeals judgement in paragraph 237. With this, I believe, Your Honours, we can safely leave the field of military jargon and return to applying the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Your Honours, I would like now to go into the closed session because I want to make some submissions on testimony that was in closed session, with your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A very brief question: The third-last paragraph you mentioned from the judgement, and you can read it on today's transcript, page 147, line 9 to 10. There it reads that "In paragraph 474 of the judgement, Defence Witness Marin confirmed that the situation got worse after the appellant so-called issued preventive orders." Reading this in context, I was desperately looking for some kind of evidence supporting this, and I would ask you if you could assist me in this search, because in its entirety the paragraph reads: "Admittedly the accused did give an order on 18 January 1993 for the attention of the regular units of the HVO, the independent units, and military police force battalion, instructing them to make sure that all soldiers prone to criminal conduct were not in a position to do any harm." Then comes your sentence: "However, that order remained without effect, even though the accused issued a reminder on 6 February 1993. On the contrary, according to the Witness Marin, the situation deteriorated thereafter," without any concrete quote or supporting evidence. And it continues: "The Defence also presented an order issued by the accused on 17 March 1993 requiring the commanders of all HVO brigades to identify the members who were prone to criminal conduct." Please assist me with this. Do you have any evidence with the deluge of paperwork we have before us, supporting this testimony of Witness Marin that the situation, in fact, deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for your question. I am unable to assist you immediately on this question. But the manner in which we read the assessment made by the Trial Chamber in this case is that -- is as follows: The Trial Chamber had before it several so-called preventative or humanitarian orders issued by the appellant. This was in evidence before the Trial Chamber. We also know that the appellant has adduced some of these so-called preventative or humanitarian orders on appeal. The manner in which I believe the Trial Chamber dealt with this evidence is that it took into account that these orders were issued, but in the end the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that most of these orders were issued after an event had happened, after the appellant had been ordered, for instance, by his superiors to look for criminals, or after there had been a humanitarian outcry. There is very little evidence on record that the appellant issued genuine preventative orders. Your Honours, also - and this is what the Trial Chamber -- I can't find the paragraph right away - but the Trial Chamber in the end came to the conclusion that the appellant never ensured that his so-called preventative orders were followed up. If he had, he would not have continued to redeploy these troops for further operations. But if your question goes to whether there's any support in concreto for Slavko Marin's testimony, with kind permission, I will return to your question tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to this, the question remains: It is still your opinion that those orders mentioned there should be from your point of view seen as more or less sham orders?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, it is a difficult question, because, of course, I have not been involved in the trial. But I can only repeat my impression, which is based on the assessment of the Trial Chamber, that as many accused before this Tribunal, there is always some evidence, for instance, that some accused helped some victims from the other side. In this case, the accused had gone through military training. He had followed courses from the Red Cross. He knew what he had to do. But in the end, he went ahead, regardless of whether or not crimes were committed, regardless of whether or not his subordinates or units he gave orders to complied with these orders. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I think we should break now. It's quarter to 6.00. We can perhaps break for 20 minutes and have still almost one hour to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please be seated. Well, I give the floor to the Prosecution. Mr. Farrell? Or again Ms. Boelaert-Suominen. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOELAERT-SUOMINEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will take just one minute of your time to provide the Prosecution's response to the appellant's ground of appeal relating to the defective indictment, insofar as Article 7(1) and 7(3) is concerned: The Prosecution adopts its written submissions in total on this issue, but we only refer to a additional authority, which can be found in the Krnojelac appeal judgement which was rendered recently. And in paragraph 138 of that judgement, the Chamber has confirmed that it is vital for the indictment to specify at least on what legal basis of the Statute an individual is being charged. And then it says in brackets either Article 7(1) and/or 7(3). Without wishing to oversimplify matters, Your Honours, this is just an additional authority for the position taken by the Prosecution in its respondent's brief. Also refer to other authority. Your Honours, I would like to make it clear that the Prosecution does not accept that the Trial Chamber in this case decided that the indictment would be fatally defective. The Trial Chamber, in the decision of the 23rd of May, 1997, stated that it would not fail to draw all necessary consequences if it would come to the conclusion that the appellant would not have been able to present an effective legal defence on all counts. Two years on, the Trial Chamber came to the conclusion that there was no prejudice and that the Defence had been able to present an effective legal defence, Your Honours. I would also refer you to the case of Colak v. Germany, before the European Court of Human Rights, which goes to a point which we have drawn attention to in our respondent's brief. In this case, European Court of Human Rights confirmed that an accused can derive no rights from comments made during trial proceedings. If these comments are not accompanied by a statement that a certain charge or a count would be withdrawn. The case is in our book of authorities, Your Honours. We rely on this case to state that likewise, to the extent that the appellant claims that the Presiding Judge would have misled him regarding the question of whether this was a 7(1) case or a 7(3) case, the comment cannot be relied upon. This concludes the Prosecution's oral submissions in relation to the defective indictment issue, Your Honours. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Boelaert-Suominen. And Mr. Farrell, you have now the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If you can't hear me, I'm going to be moving with some material, so please let me know. I'll be dealing with the -- some of the factual matters, not all of the factual matters that were raised by my learned colleagues, and I will be dealing shortly with the allegations of Rule 68 violation. But before I do, there's something quite puzzling about this case. It's not simply the contradictions of the appellant's position in some respects, where he can issue humanitarian orders but he can't issue combat orders, where he can compel people to do things but he can't compel them not to do things, where he doesn't have the military police actually attached to him, but he's issuing orders to them anyway. Despite all those puzzling aspects of the Defence case, there's another one that in my respectful submission is one that you'll have to keep in mind when you assess the evidence in light of the Defence position, and that is that the one person who would know whether or not Dario Kordic was interfering with his work was affecting his ability to carry out combat operations, was affecting his ability to properly utilise troops would be the commander of the Central Bosnia operative zone, and that is Colonel Blaskic. As you listen to the -- as you listened to the evidence last week, and as you assess it this week, I'd ask that you keep in mind that it was Colonel Blaskic who was with BA3 when he was brought by the commander of the Vitezovi to his office to discuss whether or not BA3 would be released. It was Colonel Blaskic who was at the checkpoint when the Convoy of Joy was stopped and when General Duncan spoke about the fact that the police that were present wouldn't allow the convoy through because those police reported to Dario Kordic. Did the appellant testify at trial? Being present at the very incidents that he's now relying on, did he testify at trial that he could not combat his troops because of the interference of Dario Kordic? No. Did he testify when he explained what happened in Ahmici that it was because of the intervention of Dario Kordic? No. Did he testify when he explained the incident with BA3 that he couldn't prevent Kraljevic from taking steps because Kraljevic didn't report to him? No. I'll come to that testimony, but what he said is, in his testimony, when he describes the very incident that the Defence have put forward to you, where BA3 goes to his office and Blaskic has to make a telephone call, what's his testimony? His testimony is that we solved it. We, not Dario Kordic, not others outside of my command and control, but we. When you consider the evidence that you've heard, when you consider the submissions, when you consider all the documents, consider the fact that the person who knew, the one person who was in a position to raise this issue, to say: All the evidence you've heard, this is evidence where I had no control over my subordinates, was never raised. I would respectfully submit that that's very telling and that as you assess all the evidence and as you listen to the submissions, what you're left with is not new evidence. Colonel Blaskic has not put forward new evidence. It's very interesting that the actual evidence of the appellant is not that there was problems with Kordic. There's none of that on the record. The actual evidence of the appellant is not that it was Dario Kordic. The evidence of the appellant was that he couldn't control it because they were assigned to Mostar. What you're hearing is actually out of the mouths of his lawyers, his lawyers telling you that there was other evidence that should cause you to reconsider the evidence that was before the Trial Chamber. But all I'd ask you to remember is when you're assessing that evidence, remember the words of the appellant himself. He did not complain about Dario Kordic. In fact, the one time where he was asked specifically, did Dario Kordic commit the crime in Ahmici, he said: I don't know. He's not in the chain of command. He doesn't have military authority. So I just don't know. Is that consistent with the position that's being taken now with the outrage expressed by the fact that Dario Kordic seems to be everywhere in Central Bosnia, having control over every crime? With respect, it's clearly not. When you consider the evidence, consider the fact that what they were doing was working together. Clearly, there's no doubt that Dario Kordic at certain times exerted his influence and power. That's taken for granted. The evidence was before the Kordic trial, the evidence was before this trial. General Duncan testified in this trial, in the Blaskic trial, that at the Convoy of Joy, the police at the checkpoint said that they would not follow Blaskic's orders. If you look at General Duncan's testimony, Blaskic was there. Blaskic was present with him at the time. So we ever hear Blaskic saying: Here, this is the perfect example. I have to come forward and in my eight weeks of testimony I am going to raise this? We hear it from the mouths of the lawyers. We don't hear it from the mouth of the appellant, and I'd ask that you keep this in mind as you're assessing the value of this evidence. The first thing I'd like to address is the short legal submissions that were made by Mr. Hayman, and I'll simply address them briefly. The appellant has indicated that there should be a different standard in this case than in all other cases that relate to errors of fact. I simply submit that much of the argument that he made was made when we argued the Kupreskic appeal. In the Kupreskic appeal, we heard seven witnesses, as we have heard here. Certainly, much less documents, but many, many more additional evidence motions. There are dozens. And in that case, the Appeals Chamber determined that the standard was that the burden is on the appellant to establish that no reasonable tribunal of fact could have reached a conclusion of guilt based on the evidence before the Trial Chamber, together with the additional evidence admitted during the proceedings. I respectfully submit that it's not for this Court to look at all the evidence on the trial record de novo. It's a very interesting twist. The appellant's counsel says because of the fact that you will have to decide issues of credibility in relation to the six witnesses, you actually should exercise your authority to hear the whole case de novo. In other words, determine issues of credibility in relation to all the other witness. Well, if it's going to be difficult to assess the six in light of all the other evidence, I surmise it would be much more difficult to assess the credibility of all the others that you haven't heard. And it's not outside this Court's jurisdiction and certainly the exercise of its authority to determine matters when you don't hear witnesses. The courts in this Tribunal certainly hear matters through Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: There are 70 documents before you. Of those 70 documents, you have not heard any witnesses. Many of the documents that are before you come from intelligence services, and the Defence relies on them extensively. Many of them are unsourced, many of them are unsigned. But you're in a position, and of course the parties trust the Court, to assess the value, the credibility, and the weight to be given to those documents. Issues relating to the credibility or the weight to be given to those documents can be made without calling witnesses, in light of a number of other factors, whether they're corroborated, whether they're internally consistent, the timing in which they're made, the normal factors that you would consider as Judges. The appellant also indicates that a second reason why this Court should apply a different standard is because of the alleged Rule 68 violation. With respect, they misconstrue the issue. The issue is what to do with the evidence when it's before you, not does the manner in which it comes before you or the reason why it was not available at trial affect the standard you should apply. With respect, that would be the wrong approach. If this Court determines that there is a Rule 68 violation, it has to determine whether or not that violation withheld evidence or if the evidence which is now before you could have had an impact on the verdict. That can be done, fortunately, in our system because of Rule 115. That evidence can be brought before you and you can make an assessment and this Court can sanction the Prosecution or take steps if it feels there's a Rule 68 violation. But that's different than the standard you would apply when the evidence is brought before you, in my respectful submission. I'll now turn to the allegations regarding Rule 68. In the Prosecution's submission, it's somewhat difficult to actually assess what the allegation is in relation to Rule 68. We're certainly aware of the allegations in relation to Witness Watkins, and we're aware that there are allegations that B1 - sorry - BA1, BA3, BA5, and the Witness Watkins are Rule 68 violations. If I recall Mr. Hayman's submissions correctly, he said, and there are a number of documents in the second Rule 115 motion which we've identified. Well, with respect, it would certainly be an attempt to address any allegations of Rule 68. But if that's the submission of the appellant, then the onus is on him, I would respectfully submit, to at least identify what the -- what the Rule 68 violations are so the Prosecution can address them. Secondly, the appellant only raised three specific incidents in his appeal brief regarding Rule 68 violations, and they weren't -- the only one that was raised in relation to the material I've just pointed out was BA1. He didn't raise in his appeal brief the other matters. In the last sentence of the section, he indicates that he incorporates by reference all other submissions and all other violations of Rule 68. With respect, if he didn't put them in his appeal brief, he didn't brief them and indicate which ones he was relying on for the purposes of the appeal. It's difficult for the Prosecution to try to respond to these very serious allegations that Mr. Hayman made so eloquently before you this morning. But then at the end, he didn't identify which passages he was relying on, didn't identify which documents, and didn't identify what the prejudice was. I will try to address the issues that are raised in relation to the identified BA1, BA3, BA5, and Mr. Watkins. Of course, the Prosecution is at your disposal, if you request written submissions afterwards, if there are any other matters raised in the reply by the appellant which I have not addressed. In relation to BA5, there's an allegation of a Rule 68 violation in the failure to disclose the evidence of BA5. As you'll recall, BA5 was the person who testified last week who was in Stari Vitez and who testified in the Kordic trial. According to my records, BA5's statement was disclosed in 1996 to the appellant, and this was noted in the Prosecution's response to the second Rule 115 motion, attached to our second -- our response to the second Rule 115 motion are documents demonstrating that BA5's statement was disclosed at that time to the Defence. His date of testimony, as far as I can ascertain, is after the judgement in this case. So the statement was disclosed, he testified after the judgement; so therefore, any Rule 68 violation certainly didn't occur at trial. I also would note that in relation to BA5, on the motion under Rule 115, this Chamber admitted BA5's anticipated testimony in the interests of justice. And I interpret that to mean, in light of the other aspects that were admitted, that it was found that it was available -- the evidence was available to the appellant at the time. So if the statement was disclosed during trial, the statement is the substance of the testimony, and the Court has found that the witness was available and could have been called by the appellant during trial, there certainly was no violation of Rule 68 at trial, and to the extent that there was a violation in the sense that immediately after trial it wasn't disclosed to the appellant, there certainly doesn't appear to be any prejudice at this stage. Now, I'll turn to BA3. BA3, as you'll recall, testified last week, and he had given a statement, as I understand, in 1995. This statement was disclosed to the Defence in November 1996. And, as I'm sure my colleagues will recall, there was an e-mail exchange in 1996 back and forth about BA3's statement because the Defence was of the view that it appeared there was a page missing. There was four or five letters that went back and forth, and the full statement, as the Prosecution had it, was disclosed to the Defence in 1996 in this trial. BA3 testified on the 19th, 25th, and 26th of January, 2000. As far as the Prosecution can ascertain, any violation of Rule 68 arose from January 26th, 2000 until disclosure. But the statement and the substance of the evidence for BA3 was disclosed back in 1996. Once again, though it doesn't necessarily alleviate the Prosecution, clearly, of its Rule 68 obligations, this Court found, on its determination under Rule 115, that this evidence was available to the Defence but granted the admission of this material in the interests of justice. Now I'll turn to BA1. It's my understanding that BA1 gave a statement in August 1996, and he testified on the 8th of November, 1999. According to the records that I've been able to ascertain, I think it's clear the Prosecution did not disclose the statement of BA1 to the Defence during trial from the date that it was taken, which was in 1996. I think that's clear on the record, and the Prosecution acknowledges it. The question then becomes: When did the appellant obtain the transcripts of BA1, and what prejudice arose? The appellant obtained the transcripts on their own - that's clear - it appears in December 1999. For their own good due diligence they were able to obtain it because it was public session material during the Kordic trial, and they obtained it by going to a website and obtaining the material and taking down the evidence of BA1. And then they subsequently, after they filed their notice of appeal, they filed a motion with the Court asking that the Prosecution be found in violation of Rule 68 because it hadn't disclosed certain information. It was evident on the motion that they actually had the material since before the judgement came out. The judgement came out in March 2000. They had the material, which they obtained on their own, in December 1999. The Appeals Chamber rendered a decision on this matter. And this is in relation specifically to BA1's testimony. The Appeals Chamber states that -- and this is in the decision of September 26, 2000, Prosecutor versus Tihomir Blaskic, decision on the appellant's motions for the production of material, suspension or extension of the briefing schedule, and additional filings. I think, Mr. President, you were the only one sitting on the Bench at that time. In paragraph 37 of that decision, it states: "The Appeals Chamber notes that in respect of the Prosecution's second reason, the appellant's counsel knew of the existence of the evidence that might exculpate the appellant soon after the evidence was given in open court at the Tribunal, yet he remained silent before the Trial Chamber until the production motion was filed on appeal. There has been no explanation from the appellant as to why he remained reticent, in spite of this information. A fact concerning the question as to whether the appellant was capable of ordering certain units of the HVO to attack villages and towns should have alerted any diligent counsel so that he or she would bring it to the attention of the Trial Chamber." In the next paragraph, the Court has to address the situation as to whether or not the Prosecution is alleviated of its Rule 68 obligation when material is found in the public domain. And the Court, quite understandably, indicates that: "The Appeals Chamber considers that the Prosecution may still be relieved of the obligation under Rule 68 if the existence of the relevant exculpatory evidence is known and the evidence is accessible to the appellant, as the appellant would not be prejudiced materially by this violation." It appears what the Court is saying is it is a violation. It clearly is a technical violation. That seems to be the case here in respect to BA1. But what the Court finds, this Court, relating to BA1, in this instance, has found that the appellant is not materially prejudiced by this violation. So, granted, if the Court is of the view that the -- excuse me -- the Court has found, I think it's fair to say, in the decision in September 26th, that there was a violation of some sort, a technical violation, by the failure to disclose it. But they balance that with the fact that it's in the public domain, the appellant knows about it and has access to it and can't come back which is what they did three months later and bring a motion alleging a violation of Rule 68 and seeking some sort of remedy. I would note, if I may just go into closed session for one minute. I'm going to refer to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We'll go to private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar, for noticing. The Trial Chamber found that on the 16th of April, the Croatian forces, commanded by Colonel Blaskic, attacked in the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca. They attacked Vitez, Stari Vitez, Ahmici, Nadioci, Santici, Pirici, Navoci, Putis, and Donja Veceriska. Now, the only real - I say "real" in quotation marks - the only new "real" additional evidence that's put forward by the appellant to claim that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in its finding that the HVO initiated an attack on that morning are documents from the ABiH army itself and the appellant's own war diary. Now, if the appellant is issuing preparatory orders the night before for an all-out attack in 20 places, it's not necessarily inconsistent to imagine that he's going to tell his duty officer to ensure that what's written in the war diary is consistent with his preparatory orders. I can't imagine he's going to initiate an attack throughout Central Bosnia and tell his operations officer to record that the ABiH is on the defensive and is being attacked by the HVO, while still issue orders which he said are orders to reflect that the HVO may be attacked. And you'll recall, and I'll come back to it, the evidence of BA3 in that regard, and the troops that he described that was on the axis. In fact, BA3 gave a very interesting answer. In the hypothetical, as to whether or not, if he was in Colonel Blaskic's shoes and he received an intelligence report that the ABiH army was moving through an axis route to engage in an attack the next morning on Ahmici, he indicated that he would do the same thing. But when asked whether or not it was in fact true that this factual circumstance existed, he went on to explain that the members of the territorial force defending the area were poorly manned, had hunting rifles. There is ample trial evidence in support of the findings, and I won't go through it, but there are a number of witnesses and there's a number of international -- both local and international, and a number of reports as to the initiation of the attack by the HVO on the morning of the 16th. All the witnesses that came before you have spoken about this issue. BA3, BA5, and even BA2 indicated that it was the HVO that initiated the attack. The appellant has attempted to rely on ABiH documents in an effort to demonstrate that in fact it was the ABiH that initiated an attack. In fact, I reviewed their submissions in this regard, and I'm going to refer to their documents 12 and 13 of the fourth additional evidence motion. And I was uncertain as to whether they were relying on them to indicate that there were ABiH forces in Ahmici or whether they were saying that this demonstrates that there was an attack. In referring to document 12 -- excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I was wondering whether the AV people could put the computer evidence on the screen so that it might be visible to Your Honours. I'd just try to put PA12 and PA13 on screen so that you wouldn't have to find them. I'm sorry, yes, the Defence Exhibits 12 and 13. It doesn't appear that we can get them on screen, so I'll try and explain them to you. If you like, I can try and put one on the ELMO. That may be of assistance. Hopefully you'll be able to see the document. This document, as I understand from the Defence's fourth additional evidence motion, was put forward to indicate that Blaskic's order at 1.30 in the morning on the 16th - well, which is the night of the 15th, the morning of the 16th - but this order by Colonel Blaskic was a preparatory order, and it was just the flipside of this order; in other words, both the ABiH and the HVO were on alert and, therefore, they both were issuing preparatory orders. If I could just ask, sir, if we could go to see the top of the document. That's great. Thank you. The Defence have put it forward for the proposition that this is a preparatory order, the same as Blaskic's, and it just shows that both sides are preparing in case of anything occurring. If you look at the first sentences -- the first sentence, Your Honours, it says: "In accordance with the unfolding of events, and in connection with the attack by the HVO unit on units of the BiH -- or the BH army in the zone of responsibility of the 325th Brigade, and the newly arisen situation, the corps command is taking measures." Then, in the next paragraph, there's comments about having to be in readiness to assist the BH forces in villages, including Ahmici. And then in the first subparagraph, it indicates that a company has been sent to the Ahmici village sector with the task to organise and carry out a march and arrive in the Ahmici village sector to assist their forces. This, in my respectful submission, does not indicate that the ABiH attacked the HVO, and it doesn't indicate that it's some type of preparatory order similar to the ones referred to by the appellant. The first line indicates that there's been an attack by HVO. The other thing which is interesting about this order is if you -- you can see on the screen that it says the "16th of April, 1993." And the appellant has indicated that this would demonstrate that on the same day, at the same time, that the ABiH is taking the same preparatory measures for possible attacks. What hasn't been translated from the B/C/S is, in fact, the date of this order, when it was sent. The B/C/S has a date-stamp on the third page, which indicates that it was sent on the 17th of April, at 2.12 in the morning, at 2.12 a.m., which is completely consistent with the ABiH responding after an attack on the 16th. This matter was sent to the forces on the 17th. If I can ask that Defence Exhibit 13 be put on the ELMO, and then I'll finish, Mr. President, after reference to this. The Defence also rely on this order from the ABiH for the same purpose. If you look in the first paragraph, it says: "Based on the latest developments and conduct of the Croatian Defence Council units, and with a view to precluding any surprise or initiative-taking by the HVO," and it says, "in keeping with the order of the 3rd Corps" -- it then refers to a number, 02/33-872. That is the number of the previous order, which went out on the 17th. It says: "In keeping with the previous order" -- and the number there, if you flip back -- if you had document 12 before you, you would see that document 12 is actually that document with that order number, that actually went out on the morning of the 17th. So once again, though it says the 16th on the morning, it obviously has to be sent after receiving the previous order. Within the body of the order, without going through it, it does indicate that one company has the task of reaching the village of Ahmici as soon as possible and joining in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May we break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: By way of a compromise reached in the Bench, we will start tomorrow morning at 8.45. The Prosecution is still entitled, according to my calculation, to one hour and 50 minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: -- for its submissions. The hearing stands adjourned.
